cases.title: Young Woman with Recurrent Kidney Stones
learning_objectives: Understand metabolic workup for recurrent stones
Differentiate stone types and prevention strategies
cases.presentation: 28-year-old woman with sudden onset severe left flank pain radiating to groin

history.chief_complaint: Worst pain of my life in my left side and back
history.hpi: Patient awoke with sudden severe left flank pain radiating to left groin and labia. Pain is colicky, comes in waves, 10/10 severity. Associated with nausea and vomiting. Some gross hematuria noted. Cannot find comfortable position. This is her fourth kidney stone episode in 3 years. Prior stones passed spontaneously but required ER visits for pain control. Family history notable for multiple relatives with kidney stones.
history.pmh: Recurrent nephrolithiasis, no other medical problems
history.social: Marketing executive, high-stress job, admits poor fluid intake, non-smoker
history.family: Mother, maternal grandmother, and two maternal aunts all have history of kidney stones

physical_exam.general: In severe distress, writhing in pain, unable to lie still
physical_exam.abdomen: Soft, non-distended, left CVA tenderness, no peritoneal signs

labs.24hr_urine: High calcium (>250 mg/day), low citrate (<320 mg/day), high oxalate, normal uric acid, low urine volume (1.2 L/day)

imaging.ct_abdomen_pelvis_noncontrast: 5mm stone at left ureterovesical junction causing mild hydronephrosis. Multiple small non-obstructing stones in bilateral kidneys. Stone density 800 Hounsfield units (consistent with calcium oxalate).

cases.explanation: Recurrent calcium oxalate nephrolithiasis. Key features: (1) Classic renal colic: sudden severe colicky flank pain radiating to groin, (2) Hematuria, (3) Four episodes in 3 years with family history (suggests metabolic etiology), (4) Metabolic workup shows: hypercalciuria, hypocitraturia, hyperoxaluria, low urine volume, (5) CT shows obstructing stone at UVJ plus multiple non-obstructing bilateral stones. Calcium oxalate stones are most common (70-80%). Stone <5mm: 90% pass spontaneously; 5-10mm: 50% pass; >10mm: rarely pass.
management_pearls: ACUTE management: NSAIDs (ketorolac 30mg IV) superior to opioids for renal colic, IV fluids, antiemetics, alpha-blocker (tamsulosin 0.4mg daily) for medical expulsive therapy
Urology referral if: stone >10mm, severe obstruction with AKI, infected stone (pyonephrosis), intractable pain, solitary kidney
Intervention options: Shock wave lithotripsy (ESWL) for stones <2cm, ureteroscopy with laser lithotripsy, percutaneous nephrolithotomy for large stones

PREVENTION (metabolic syndrome for recurrent stones): Increase fluid intake to 2.5-3L/day (goal urine output >2L/day), potassium citrate 10-20 mEq BID-TID (increases urinary citrate, alkalinizes urine), thiazide diuretic (hydrochlorothiazide 25mg daily) for hypercalciuria, limit sodium to <2g/day, normal calcium diet (low calcium paradoxically increases stones), limit oxalate-rich foods (spinach, nuts, chocolate, tea)
Stone analysis after passage - guides future prevention
pitfalls: Don't assume pain is from old kidney stone - always image to exclude other etiologies and assess for obstruction
Pregnant women with suspected stones: ultrasound first, avoid CT radiation
Infected obstructed stone (pyonephrosis): fever + stone = emergency urologic decompression (percutaneous nephrostomy or stent) + antibiotics
Common stone types: Calcium oxalate (70%), calcium phosphate (5-10%), uric acid (5-10%, radiolucent), struvite (10%, 'staghorn', associated with infection), cystine (1%, genetic)

cases.title: Patient with Facial Droop and Inability to Close Eye
learning_objectives: Recognize upper vs lower motor neuron facial paralysis
Understand treatment and prognosis of Bell's palsy
cases.presentation: 42-year-old woman with sudden onset right facial weakness and inability to close right eye

history.chief_complaint: Right side of my face is drooping and I can't close my right eye
history.hpi: Patient woke up this morning with right facial weakness. Noticed when brushing teeth that she couldn't spit properly - water dribbled out right side of mouth. Cannot close right eye completely. Taste seems off on right side of tongue. Mild pain behind right ear yesterday. No headache, no limb weakness, no speech difficulty, no vision changes. Had upper respiratory infection last week.
history.social: Teacher, non-smoker, no alcohol

physical_exam.cranial_nerves: CN VII (Facial): Right facial weakness involving entire right side of face - cannot raise right eyebrow, cannot wrinkle right forehead, cannot close right eye completely (lagophthalmos), right nasolabial fold flattened, mouth deviates to left when smiling. Taste decreased on right anterior tongue. Hyperacusis on right (increased sensitivity to sound). CN II-VI, VIII-XII: intact.
physical_exam.sensory: Intact to light touch and pinprick

imaging.mri_brain: Not routinely indicated, but if done would show normal (no stroke)

cases.explanation: Bell's palsy (idiopathic facial nerve palsy) is acute unilateral lower motor neuron facial weakness. Key features: (1) Sudden onset unilateral facial weakness affecting ENTIRE side of face including forehead (cannot raise eyebrow or wrinkle forehead), (2) Inability to completely close eye, (3) Associated features: hyperacusis, altered taste, retroauricular pain, (4) No limb weakness or speech difficulty (differentiates from stroke), (5) Recent viral URI (HSV-1 reactivation suspected). Upper motor neuron lesion (stroke) SPARES forehead due to bilateral innervation - key differentiating feature.
management_pearls: Corticosteroids within 72 hours: Prednisone 60mg daily x 5-7 days, then taper (improves recovery)
Antivirals controversial but often given: Valacyclovir 1000mg TID x 7 days (if started within 72 hours)
Eye protection critical: Artificial tears during day, lubricating ointment at night, eye patch or taping eye closed at night (prevent corneal abrasion/ulceration)
Physical therapy: Facial exercises to prevent contracture
Prognosis: 70% complete recovery, 85% substantial recovery, 15% permanent weakness. Incomplete eye closure at 1 week predicts poorer outcome.
Follow-up in 1 week to assess improvement, ophthalmology if corneal exposure
pitfalls: STROKE vs BELL'S PALSY: Stroke spares forehead (can wrinkle forehead, raise eyebrow), Bell's affects entire face including forehead
Ramsay Hunt syndrome: Facial palsy + vesicular rash in ear/oral cavity + severe pain (VZV reactivation) - needs acyclovir, worse prognosis
Lyme disease: Can cause facial palsy (often bilateral), check if endemic area or outdoor exposure
Bilateral facial palsy: Consider Guillain-Barré syndrome, Lyme disease, sarcoidosis - not typical Bell's palsy
If facial weakness progresses or other neurologic signs develop - imaging to rule out tumor, stroke

Differentiate systolic vs diastolic heart failure
Understand acute management of decompensated heart failure
cases.presentation: 68-year-old man with progressive shortness of breath, orthopnea, and bilateral leg swelling

history.chief_complaint: Can't catch my breath and my legs are so swollen I can't put on shoes
history.hpi: Patient reports progressive shortness of breath over past 2 weeks. Initially only with exertion, now dyspneic at rest. Sleeps on 3 pillows due to orthopnea (usually uses 1). cases.explanation: Acute decompensated heart failure (ADHF) with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF). Key features: (1) Progressive dyspnea, orthopnea, PND (left heart failure symptoms), (2) Volume overload: leg edema, JVD, hepatomegaly, weight gain (right heart failure signs), (3) Pulmonary edema on exam (crackles) and CXR, (4) S3 gallop (ventricular filling dysfunction), (5) Markedly elevated BNP, (6) Severely reduced EF 25%, (7) Precipitants: medication non-compliance, dietary indiscretion (high sodium), AFib with RVR. This is acute-on-chronic systolic heart failure decompensation.
management_pearls: IMMEDIATE: Oxygen, upright position, continuous monitoring
IV loop diuretics: Furosemide 40-80mg IV bolus (or 2.5x home oral dose), then continuous infusion if needed. Goal: net negative 0.5-1L daily, weight loss 1-2 lbs/day
Monitor: Daily weights, strict I&O, electrolytes (especially potassium and magnesium with diuresis), renal function
If inadequate diuresis: Add thiazide (metolazone) for synergy, increase furosemide dose, consider IV inotropes (dobutamine) or vasodilators (nitroglycerin, nitroprusside)
Rate control for AFib: Continue/optimize beta-blocker when euvolemic
Resume guideline-directed medical therapy once euvolemic: ACE-I/ARB or ARNI (sacubitril/valsartan), beta-blocker, aldosterone antagonist, SGLT2 inhibitor
Address precipitants: Medication compliance, dietary sodium restriction (<2g/day), fluid restriction (<2L/day if hyponatremia)
Disposition: Admit if: hypoxia, significant azotemia, symptomatic hypotension, inadequate oral diuresis, need for IV therapy
pitfalls: BNP >500: heart failure likely. BNP 100-500: gray zone. BNP <100: HF unlikely. (Note: BNP lower in obesity, higher in renal failure)
Aggressive diuresis can worsen renal function ('cardiorenal syndrome') - balance fluid removal with maintaining perfusion
Don't stop beta-blocker acutely - can cause rebound tachycardia and worsening. May need to down-titrate temporarily if severe decompensation.
HFrEF vs HFpEF: Reduced EF (<40%) vs preserved EF (>50%). HFpEF is diastolic dysfunction - treatment differs (less evidence for medications)

cases.explanation: Streptococcal pharyngitis (strep throat) caused by Group A Streptococcus is common in young adults. Key features: (1) Sudden onset sore throat with fever, (2) Tonsillar exudates and erythema, (3) Tender anterior cervical lymphadenopathy, (4) ABSENCE of cough/rhinorrhea (suggests viral if present), (5) Centor score 4/4 (fever, exudates, tender LAD, no cough) = 50% probability strep. Positive rapid strep confirms diagnosis. Untreated strep can lead to rheumatic fever and post-strep glomerulonephritis.
management_pearls: Centor criteria (1 point each): Fever, Tonsillar exudates, Tender anterior cervical LAD, Absence of cough. Score 0-1: no testing/treatment (viral likely), Score 2-3: rapid strep test, Score 4: treat empirically or test
Treatment: Penicillin V 500mg PO BID x 10 days OR Amoxicillin 500mg TID x 10 days (first-line, cheap, narrow spectrum)
PCN allergy: Azithromycin 500mg day 1, then 250mg days 2-5 OR Cephalexin 500mg BID x 10 days (if not severe allergy)
Symptomatic relief: NSAIDs, throat lozenges, warm salt water gargles
Return to work/school after 24 hours on antibiotics and fever-free
Complications if untreated: acute rheumatic fever (2-3 weeks), post-strep glomerulonephritis (1-3 weeks), peritonsillar abscess
pitfalls: Viral pharyngitis is 5-10x more common than strep - don't over-prescribe antibiotics
Mononucleosis: Tonsillar exudates + posterior cervical LAD + fatigue + splenomegaly. Avoid amoxicillin (causes rash in mono)
Peritonsillar abscess: Unilateral findings, uvular deviation, trismus, 'hot potato voice' - needs ENT drainage
Complete 10-day antibiotic course to prevent rheumatic fever (even if symptoms improve)

cases.explanation: Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) is extremely common, affecting 20% of adults. Key features: (1) Burning retrosternal chest pain (heartburn), (2) Worse after meals and when supine, (3) Acid regurgitation/sour taste, (4) Relief with antacids, (5) Risk factors: obesity, smoking, large meals, alcohol, NSAIDs, late-night eating. Lower esophageal sphincter dysfunction allows stomach acid to reflux into esophagus. Diagnosis is clinical - no testing needed for typical symptoms without alarm features.
management_pearls: Lifestyle modifications FIRST: weight loss if obese, elevate head of bed 6-8 inches, avoid late meals (3 hours before bed), stop smoking, limit alcohol/caffeine/fatty foods/chocolate/peppermint/citrus, small frequent meals
Medical therapy: PPI (proton pump inhibitor) is first-line. Omeprazole 20mg daily 30 min before breakfast x 8 weeks. Other PPIs: pantoprazole, esomeprazole, lansoprazole
H2 blockers (ranitidine, famotidine): less effective than PPIs but reasonable for mild/intermittent symptoms
If no response to PPI: increase to BID dosing (before breakfast and dinner), ensure taking 30 min before meals, rule out non-compliance
Successful treatment: taper PPI to lowest effective dose, consider on-demand therapy
Long-term PPI risks: C. diff, pneumonia, osteoporosis, B12/magnesium deficiency - use lowest dose needed
pitfalls: Alarm symptoms requiring urgent EGD: dysphagia, odynophagia, weight loss, GI bleeding, anemia, family history of GI cancer, age >60 with new-onset symptoms
Cardiac chest pain mimics GERD - if ANY cardiac risk factors or atypical features, work up for ACS first
Barrett's esophagus: intestinal metaplasia from chronic GERD, precancerous. Screen with EGD if chronic GERD >5 years + male + white + age >50 + obesity + smoking + family history
Refractory GERD: consider non-compliance, inadequate PPI dosing, delayed gastric emptying, eosinophilic esophagitis, functional heartburn

cases.explanation: Essential (primary) hypertension affects 30% of US adults. Key features: (1) Sustained elevated BP ≥130/80 on multiple occasions, (2) No secondary cause identified, (3) Risk factors: obesity, sedentary lifestyle, high sodium diet, smoking, family history, (4) Usually asymptomatic (silent killer), (5) Stage 2 HTN (≥140/90) requires lifestyle + medication. Diagnosis requires: elevated BP on ≥2 occasions on ≥2 separate visits OR home BP monitoring confirming HTN. This patient has Stage 2 HTN with multiple cardiovascular risk factors.
management_pearls: BP Classification: Normal <120/80, Elevated 120-129/<80, Stage 1 HTN 130-139/80-89, Stage 2 HTN ≥140/90
Stage 2 HTN: Lifestyle modifications PLUS medication. Stage 1: lifestyle first if ASCVD risk <10%, medication if risk ≥10%
Lifestyle: DASH diet (low sodium <2g/day, high K+), weight loss (1mm Hg per kg lost), exercise 150 min/week, limit alcohol (≤2 drinks/day men, ≤1 women), smoking cessation
First-line medications: Thiazide diuretic (HCTZ, chlorthalidone), ACE inhibitor (lisinopril), ARB (losartan), or CCB (amlodipine). This patient: ACE-I or ARB (prediabetic - renoprotective)
Start: Lisinopril 10mg daily, recheck BP in 2-4 weeks. Goal <130/80. Titrate or add second agent if needed
Monitoring: Check BMP 2-4 weeks after starting ACE-I (watch creatinine and K+), annual A1C and lipids, assess for target organ damage
pitfalls: Must confirm HTN diagnosis - single elevated reading is NOT sufficient. Home BP monitoring or repeat office measurements required
Secondary HTN causes (rare 5-10%): renal artery stenosis, primary aldosteronism, pheochromocytoma, Cushing's, OSA. Suspect if: age <30, resistant HTN, sudden onset, hypokalemia
Resistant HTN (uncontrolled on 3 agents including diuretic): check compliance, proper BP measurement technique, white coat effect, secondary causes, OSA
Target organ damage: check for LVH (EKG/echo), proteinuria (UA), retinopathy (fundoscopy), kidney disease (Cr, eGFR)

cases.explanation: Migraine is extremely common, affecting 12% of population (18% women, 6% men). Key features: (1) Severe unilateral throbbing/pulsating headache, (2) Associated symptoms: nausea/vomiting, photophobia, phonophobia, (3) Duration 4-72 hours if untreated, (4) Recurrent pattern, often menstrual, (5) Family history common, (6) Triggers: stress, hormones, foods, sleep changes, weather. Diagnosis is CLINICAL using POUND criteria (Pulsating, One-day duration, Unilateral, Nausea, Disabling) - imaging NOT needed for typical migraine.
management_pearls: ACUTE treatment (take early in attack): NSAIDs (ibuprofen 600-800mg, naproxen 500mg), Triptans (sumatriptan 100mg PO, rizatriptan 10mg ODT - abortive, most effective), Antiemetics (metoclopramide, prochlorperazine - also treat nausea)
Avoid opioids and butalbital (rebound headaches, dependence)
PREVENTIVE therapy if ≥4 headaches/month, ≥8 headache days/month, or disabling: Propranolol 80-240mg/day, Topiramate 50-200mg/day, Amitriptyline 25-100mg qHS, or CGRP inhibitors (erenumab)
Lifestyle: identify triggers (diary), regular sleep, hydration, avoid trigger foods (alcohol, aged cheese, processed meats, caffeine withdrawal), stress management
Medication overuse headache: if using abortive >10 days/month for 3+ months - wean off, start preventive
pitfalls: RED FLAGS requiring imaging: sudden thunderclap headache, new headache >50yo, progressive worsening, neurologic deficits, fever/meningismus, position-dependent, post-trauma, immunocompromised
Thunderclap headache: subarachnoid hemorrhage until proven otherwise - CT head, LP if negative CT
Migraine with aura: visual (zigzag lines, scotoma) or sensory symptoms preceding headache. Estrogen contraceptives increase stroke risk - avoid if migraine with aura
Cluster headache: brief (15-180 min), unilateral periorbital pain, autonomic symptoms (lacrimation, rhinorrhea, ptosis), occurs in clusters. Men>women. Oxygen and triptans for acute

cases.explanation: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) affects 10% of US adults and is increasing with obesity epidemic. Key features: (1) Hyperglycemia from insulin resistance and relative insulin deficiency, (2) Polyuria, polydipsia (classic symptoms), (3) Risk factors: obesity (BMI 34), sedentary lifestyle, family history, acanthosis nigricans (insulin resistance marker), (4) Diagnosis: Fasting glucose ≥126 mg/dL on 2 occasions OR HbA1c ≥6.5% OR random glucose ≥200 with symptoms. This patient meets diagnostic criteria with FG 215 and A1C 9.2%. Already has microvascular complication (microalbuminuria).
management_pearls: Goals: A1C <7% (individualize), fasting glucose 80-130, postprandial <180, BP <130/80, LDL <70 (if ASCVD)
Lifestyle first: Medical nutrition therapy (MNT) - carb counting, weight loss goal 5-7%, exercise 150 min/week, diabetes education
Metformin first-line: Start 500mg daily, titrate to 1000mg BID (max 2000mg/day). Take with meals to reduce GI side effects. Check renal function (avoid if eGFR <30)

If A1C >9% at diagnosis (like this patient): consider starting metformin PLUS second agent. Options: SGLT2 inhibitor (empagliflozin - CV/renal benefit, expensive), GLP-1 agonist (semaglutide - weight loss, CV benefit), DPP-4 inhibitor, sulfonylurea (cheap but hypoglycemia risk), insulin if very high glucose
This patient: Metformin 1000mg BID + Empagliflozin 10mg daily (renoprotective given microalbuminuria)
Monitoring: A1C every 3 months until goal, then every 6 months. Home glucose monitoring if on insulin or sulfonylurea
Screening for complications: Annual: diabetic eye exam, foot exam with monofilament, microalbuminuria, lipids. Baseline EKG.
pitfalls: Microvascular complications: retinopathy (annual dilated eye exam), nephropathy (annual microalbumin, monitor Cr/eGFR), neuropathy (annual monofilament exam, foot care education)

Macrovascular complications: ASCVD risk very high. Aspirin 81mg if ≥50yo with CV risk factor. Statin high-intensity (this patient already on statin - good). ACE-I/ARB for HTN and renal protection (already on lisinopril - good).
Hypoglycemia risk: educate on symptoms, glucose monitoring. Metformin and SGLT2i do NOT cause hypoglycemia. Sulfonylureas and insulin do.
SGLT2i precautions: risk of genital mycotic infections, DKA (rare), Fournier's gangrene (very rare). Avoid if eGFR <30. Hold during illness.
Type 1 vs Type 2: T1DM in younger patients, acute presentation, DKA, positive antibodies. Consider checking C-peptide if unclear.

cases.explanation: Acute viral gastroenteritis ('stomach flu') is extremely common. Key features: (1) Abrupt onset nausea, vomiting, watery diarrhea, (2) Crampy abdominal pain, (3) Low-grade fever, (4) Self-limited (2-3 days), (5) Outbreak setting (coworkers affected), (6) No blood in stool (viral). Antiemetics: Ondansetron 4-8mg PO/ODT (dissolving tablet) q8h PRN - helps retain fluids
Antidiarrheals: Loperamide 4mg initial, then 2mg after each loose stool (max 16mg/day). AVOID if fever or bloody diarrhea (can worsen bacterial infections)
Diet: Start bland foods when tolerated (BRAT diet: bananas, rice, applesauce, toast), advance as tolerated
IV fluids if severe dehydration or unable to tolerate PO: NS 1-2L bolus, then maintenance
This patient: Ondansetron 8mg ODT, start oral rehydration, loperamide after vomiting controlled, recheck in 24 hours or sooner if worsens
Prevention: hand hygiene, avoid food prep when ill, clean contaminated surfaces with bleach
pitfalls: RED FLAGS: bloody diarrhea, high fever >101.5°F, severe abdominal pain, signs of severe dehydration, immunocompromised, recent antibiotics, symptoms >7 days, recent travel - consider bacterial etiology, need stool studies
Bacterial gastroenteritis: Salmonella, Shigella, Campylobacter, E. coli O157:H7 - often bloody, higher fever, fecal leukocytes. May need antibiotics if severe or high-risk patient

Appendicitis: pain migrates to RLR, rebound tenderness, fever - get CT if suspicious
Dehydration severity: Mild (thirst, dry mouth), Moderate (orthostasis, tachycardia, decreased UOP), Severe (hypotension, AMS, anuric)

cases.explanation: Acute mechanical low back pain is EXTREMELY common - 80% of people experience it in lifetime. Key features: (1) Sudden onset with lifting/twisting (mechanical trigger), (2) Localized lumbar pain worse with movement, (3) NO red flags: no neurologic deficits (strength/sensation/reflexes normal), no saddle anesthesia, no bowel/bladder dysfunction, no fever, no trauma, age <50, no cancer history, no unexplained weight loss, (4) Muscle spasm and tenderness. Most cases resolve within 4-6 weeks with conservative management. Imaging is NOT helpful and often shows incidental findings leading to unnecessary interventions.
management_pearls: Conservative management is FIRST-LINE: NSAIDs (ibuprofen 600-800mg TID, naproxen 500mg BID), acetaminophen 1000mg q6h, muscle relaxants (cyclobenzaprine 5-10mg TID PRN for severe spasm)
Activity modification: avoid heavy lifting and aggravating activities, but AVOID bed rest. Stay active within pain tolerance - walking, gentle stretching. Bed rest >48 hours delays recovery.
Physical therapy referral if not improving in 2-4 weeks: core strengthening, stretching, proper lifting mechanics
Heat therapy: heating pad 20 min TID-QID for muscle relaxation
Expected course: 50% better in 1 week, 90% better in 4-6 weeks. Return to work with light duty if possible.
Return precautions: progressive weakness, numbness, bowel/bladder changes - return immediately
pitfalls: RED FLAGS requiring urgent imaging (X-ray or MRI): Age >50 with new-onset pain, significant trauma, cancer history, unexplained weight loss, fever, IV drug use, chronic steroid use, neurologic deficits (weakness, sensory loss, absent reflexes), bowel/bladder dysfunction, saddle anesthesia
Cauda equina syndrome: bilateral leg weakness, saddle anesthesia, urinary retention - SURGICAL EMERGENCY, needs urgent MRI and decompression
Radiculopathy (sciatica): leg pain > back pain, follows dermatomal pattern, positive straight leg raise - suggests disc herniation. Consider MRI if severe or not improving in 4-6 weeks.
Avoid early imaging in uncomplicated back pain - leads to unnecessary procedures, no better outcomes, higher costs
Opioids NOT recommended for acute back pain - no better than NSAIDs, addiction risk

physical_exam.lungs: Decreased breath sounds right base, crackles and bronchial breath sounds right lower lobe, egophony present, dullness to percussion right base

cases.explanation: Community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) is common in elderly and those with comorbidities. Key features: (1) Productive cough, fever, dyspnea (classic triad), (2) Pleuritic chest pain, (3) Crackles, bronchial breath sounds, egophony (consolidation), (4) CXR confirms lobar consolidation, (5) Elevated WBC with left shift, (6) Risk factors: age >65, COPD, diabetes. CURB-65 score 3 (Confusion=0, Urea>20=1, RR≥30=1, BP<90/60=0, age≥65=1) = mortality 15%, needs HOSPITALIZATION. Streptococcus pneumoniae most common (suggested by Gram-positive diplococci).
management_pearls: Severity assessment CURB-65: Confusion, Urea >20 (BUN >28), RR ≥30, BP <90 systolic or ≤60 diastolic, age ≥65. Score 0-1: outpatient, 2: consider admission, ≥3: hospitalization recommended
This patient: CURB-65=3 → ADMIT to hospital

Empiric antibiotics for hospitalized CAP (non-ICU): Beta-lactam (ceftriaxone 1g IV daily or ampicillin-sulbactam 1.5-3g IV q6h) PLUS Macrolide (azithromycin 500mg IV daily) OR Respiratory fluoroquinolone monotherapy (levofloxacin 750mg IV daily)
Start this patient: Ceftriaxone 1g IV daily + Azithromycin 500mg IV daily
Supportive care: Supplemental O2 (goal >90%), IV fluids for dehydration, antipyretics
Blood cultures before antibiotics, sputum culture if able
Typical duration: 5-7 days if clinical improvement (afebrile 48-72hrs, improving symptoms, able to take PO)
Switch to PO antibiotics when improving: Amoxicillin 1g TID or levofloxacin 750mg daily to complete course
pitfalls: Healthcare-associated pneumonia risk factors: recent hospitalization, nursing home resident, dialysis, immunosuppressed - need broader coverage for MRSA and Pseudomonas (vancomycin + piperacillin-tazobactam)
Aspiration pneumonia: impaired swallowing, alcoholism, elderly - often right lower lobe, may need anaerobic coverage (ampicillin-sulbactam or clindamycin)
Legionella: GI symptoms, hyponatremia, elevated LFTs - add fluoroquinolone, test urine antigen
Complications: parapneumonic effusion/empyema (tap if >1cm or loculated), lung abscess, respiratory failure, sepsis
Follow-up CXR in 6-8 weeks to confirm resolution, especially if smoker or age >50 (rule out underlying cancer)

physical_exam.neuro: Alert, oriented, no focal deficits

cases.explanation: Panic disorder is characterized by recurrent unexpected panic attacks. Key features: (1) Sudden onset discrete episodes of intense fear/discomfort, (2) Physical symptoms: palpitations, chest pain, dyspnea, dizziness, sweating, trembling, (3) Psychological symptoms: fear of dying, derealization, fear of losing control, (4) Peak within 10 minutes, last 20-30 minutes, (5) Recurrent attacks with worry about future attacks (anticipatory anxiety), (6) No medical cause after workup (cardiac ruled out). Affects 2-3% of population, more common in women. Diagnosis requires: recurrent unexpected attacks + ≥1 month of worry/behavioral change.
management_pearls: ACUTE panic attack: Reassurance, calm environment, breathing exercises (slow deep breaths), grounding techniques (5-4-3-2-1 sensory awareness). Benzodiazepines (lorazepam 0.5-1mg, alprazolam 0.25-0.5mg) for severe acute episodes - use sparingly due to dependence risk.
LONG-TERM management: Combination of psychotherapy + medication is most effective
Psychotherapy: Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is first-line, exposure therapy, relaxation techniques
Medications: SSRIs are first-line (sertraline 50mg daily, escitalopram 10mg daily, paroxetine 20mg daily). Takes 4-6 weeks for full effect. Start low, titrate slowly.
This patient: Start sertraline 25mg daily x 1 week, then increase to 50mg daily. Refer for CBT. Lorazepam 0.5mg PRN for breakthrough (max 2-3x/week to avoid dependence).
Lifestyle: reduce caffeine (3 cups coffee worsening anxiety), regular exercise, adequate sleep, stress management
Follow-up in 2-4 weeks to assess response, titrate medication
pitfalls: Must rule out medical causes first: cardiac (MI, arrhythmia - EKG), pulmonary (PE - rare in young healthy), endocrine (hyperthyroidism - check TSH), substance-induced (caffeine, stimulants, cocaine, withdrawal from alcohol/benzos)
Panic disorder often coexists with agoraphobia (fear/avoidance of situations where escape difficult) - ask about avoidance behaviors
Benzodiazepines provide quick relief but: tolerance develops, dependence risk, rebound anxiety with discontinuation. Use as bridge while starting SSRI, not long-term solution.
Depression commonly coexists (50-60%) - screen with PHQ-9, ask about anhedonia, sleep, appetite, suicidal ideation
Substance use: some patients self-medicate with alcohol - screen and address

cases.explanation: Acute otitis media (AOM) is extremely common in children, peak age 6-24 months. Diagnostic criteria: (1) Acute onset of symptoms, (2) Middle ear effusion (bulging TM, decreased mobility), (3) Signs of inflammation (erythema, otalgia). Risk factors: daycare, young age, recent URI, family history. Usually follows viral URI - Eustachian tube dysfunction allows bacterial invasion. Common pathogens: S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, M. catarrhalis.
management_pearls: Amoxicillin 80-90 mg/kg/day divided BID x 10 days (first-line for uncomplicated AOM)
If penicillin allergy: Azithromycin or cephalosporin (if not severe allergy)
If recent amoxicillin use or failure: Augmentin (amoxicillin-clavulanate) for beta-lactamase coverage
Pain management: Ibuprofen 10mg/kg q6h or acetaminophen 15mg/kg q4-6h
Observation without antibiotics acceptable if: >6 months old, nonsevere illness, uncertain diagnosis - follow up in 48-72 hours
Follow-up in 48-72 hours if not improving, recheck ears in 2-4 weeks
pitfalls: Otitis media with effusion (OME): fluid without infection, no antibiotics needed
Mastoiditis: postauricular swelling, erythema, ear protrusion forward - needs CT and IV antibiotics
Recurrent AOM (≥3 in 6 months or ≥4 in 1 year): consider prophylaxis or tympanostomy tubes
Tympanic membrane perforation: drainage from ear, less pain - still treat with antibiotics

Contact dermatitis (localized, not as intensely pruritic at night)
cases.explanation: Scabies is caused by Sarcoptes scabiei mite burrowing into stratum corneum. Classic presentation: intense pruritus worse at night (mite activity), characteristic distribution (finger webs, wrists, axillae, waistline, genitals, feet - spares face/head in adults). Burrows are pathognomonic. Transmitted by prolonged skin-to-skin contact. Incubation period 3-6 weeks for first infection.
management_pearls: Permethrin 5% cream: apply neck-down, wash off after 8-14 hours, repeat in 7 days
Alternative: Ivermectin 200 mcg/kg PO, repeat in 2 weeks (preferred for crusted scabies or widespread)
Treat ALL household and close contacts simultaneously (even if asymptomatic)
Wash all bedding, clothing in hot water; items that can't be washed should be sealed in plastic bag x 72 hours
Antihistamines (hydroxyzine, diphenhydramine) for pruritus relief
Pruritus may persist 2-4 weeks after successful treatment due to hypersensitivity reaction
Educate: not a hygiene issue, highly contagious, requires simultaneous treatment of contacts
pitfalls: Crusted (Norwegian) scabies: immunocompromised patients, massive mite burden, highly contagious
Post-scabetic nodules: persistent papules in groin/axillae despite cure, may need steroid injection
Treatment failure: usually due to inadequate application, not treating contacts, or reinfection
Lindane toxicity: neurotoxic, avoid in children, pregnant women, seizure disorders

cases.title: Palpitations and Irregular Pulse
learning_objectives: Recognize clinical presentation of atrial fibrillation
Understand rate vs rhythm control strategies
Calculate stroke risk and determine anticoagulation needs
Manage acute vs chronic AFib appropriately
cases.presentation: 68-year-old with palpitations, dyspnea, and irregular pulse for 2 days

history.chief_complaint: Heart racing and irregular for 2 days
history.hpi: Sudden onset palpitations 2 days ago, feels like 'heart fluttering.' Associated with dyspnea on exertion, mild fatigue, no chest pain. No syncope or presyncope. Can feel irregular heartbeat. Similar episodes in past year but resolved spontaneously within hours. This episode persisting. No recent illness, fever, or alcohol binge.
history.pmh: Hypertension, hyperlipidemia, obesity (BMI 32), obstructive sleep apnea (non-compliant with CPAP)
history.medications: Lisinopril 20mg daily, atorvastatin 40mg daily, aspirin 81mg daily
history.social: Retired, drinks 1-2 glasses wine nightly, no smoking

physical_exam.vitals: Temp 98.4°F, HR 110-140 irregular, BP 142/88, RR 18, O2 sat 96% on RA
physical_exam.cardiovascular: Irregularly irregular rhythm, no murmurs. No JVD. Peripheral pulses present.
physical_exam.general: Alert, appears anxious but comfortable at rest

imaging.ekg: Atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response (rate 120-145 bpm). No ST changes. No prior EKG for comparison.
imaging.cxr: No acute cardiopulmonary process. Normal heart size.
imaging.echocardiogram: Ordered - normal LV function (EF 55%), mild LA enlargement, no valvular disease

differential: Atrial flutter (regular sawtooth pattern vs irregularly irregular)
Multifocal atrial tachycardia (distinct P wave morphologies, often COPD patients)
Sinus tachycardia with PACs (mostly regular with occasional irregularity)
cases.explanation: Atrial fibrillation (AFib) is most common sustained arrhythmia, characterized by disorganized atrial electrical activity causing irregularly irregular ventricular response. EKG: absence of discrete P waves, irregular RR intervals. Risk factors: age, hypertension, obesity, sleep apnea, alcohol, heart failure, valvular disease. Complications: stroke (5x increased risk), heart failure, tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy. Classification: paroxysmal (<7 days, self-terminating), persistent (>7 days), permanent (accepted long-term AFib).
management_pearls: Rate control (first-line for most): Metoprolol 25-50mg BID or diltiazem 30-60mg QID, titrate to HR <110 bpm
Anticoagulation decision: Calculate CHA₂DS₂-VASc score (this patient: CHF=0, HTN=1, Age≥75=0, DM=0, Stroke=0, Vasc=0, Age 65-74=1, Sex=0 → Score=2 → anticoagulate)
Start apixaban 5mg BID or rivaroxaban 20mg daily (DOACs preferred over warfarin)
Rhythm control: Consider if young, symptomatic, first episode - cardioversion or antiarrhythmic (flecainide, amiodarone)
Cardioversion: if <48 hours duration can cardiovert without TEE; if >48 hours need 3 weeks anticoagulation or TEE to rule out thrombus
Treat underlying causes: optimize HTN control, sleep apnea treatment, weight loss, limit alcohol
Outpatient vs admission: stable, good rate control, no acute precipitant → outpatient with cardiology follow-up
pitfalls: Stroke risk: CHA₂DS₂-VASc ≥2 in men or ≥3 in women → needs anticoagulation (aspirin inadequate)
Unstable AFib: hypotension, chest pain, heart failure, or severe symptoms → urgent cardioversion
Wolff-Parkinson-White: avoid AV nodal blockers (can precipitate VFib) - needs procainamide/ibutilide
Bleeding risk: HAS-BLED score - but don't withhold anticoagulation unless very high risk and benefit low
Missed cardioversion window: >48 hours without anticoagulation → must anticoagulate 3 weeks before cardioversion or do TEE

cases.title: Fatigue, Weight Gain, and Cold Intolerance
learning_objectives: Identify subclinical hypothyroidism and treatment indications
cases.presentation: 52-year-old woman with progressive fatigue, 15-pound weight gain, and cold intolerance for 6 months

history.chief_complaint: Tired all the time, can't lose weight despite diet and exercise
history.hpi: Progressive fatigue over 6 months, sleeping 10+ hours but still exhausted. Gained 15 pounds despite eating same diet and exercising regularly. Always cold, wearing sweaters in summer. Hair thinning, skin dry. Constipation (BM every 3-4 days). Periods heavier and more irregular. Difficulty concentrating at work. Mood low. Denies depression history.
history.social: Works as accountant, stress at work attributed symptoms initially
history.family: Mother has 'thyroid problems,' sister has Hashimoto's thyroiditis

physical_exam.vitals: Temp 97.2°F, HR 56, BP 128/84, RR 12, Weight 178 lbs (was 163 lbs 6 months ago)
physical_exam.general: Overweight woman, appears fatigued, speaks slowly
physical_exam.heent: Puffy face, periorbital edema. Thyroid mildly enlarged, non-tender, no nodules. Loss of lateral third of eyebrows.
physical_exam.skin: Dry, cool skin. Hair coarse and brittle.
physical_exam.neurologic: Delayed relaxation phase of deep tendon reflexes

imaging.thyroid_ultrasound: Heterogeneous, hypoechoic appearance consistent with chronic thyroiditis. No nodules.

differential: Depression (but TSH elevated, physical findings present)
Chronic fatigue syndrome (but objective lab findings)
Menopause (age-appropriate, but hypothyroidism more likely with elevated TSH)
Anemia (can cause fatigue but doesn't explain full constellation)
Subclinical hypothyroidism (TSH 4-10, normal T4 - this patient has overt hypothyroidism)
cases.explanation: Hypothyroidism is deficient thyroid hormone production. Most common cause in US: Hashimoto's thyroiditis (autoimmune destruction, positive TPO antibodies). Classic presentation: fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance, constipation, dry skin, hair loss, bradycardia, delayed DTR relaxation. Labs: elevated TSH (most sensitive), low free T4 confirms primary hypothyroidism. Other findings: hyperlipidemia, mild anemia, hyponatremia (SIADH). Thyroid hormone regulates metabolism - deficiency slows all body systems.
management_pearls: Levothyroxine replacement: Start 1.6 mcg/kg/day (typical 75-125 mcg daily), taken on empty stomach 30-60 min before breakfast
This patient (~80 kg): Start levothyroxine 100-125 mcg daily
Monitor: Repeat TSH in 6-8 weeks, adjust dose by 12.5-25 mcg increments to achieve TSH 0.5-2.5 mIU/L
Once stable: Check TSH annually, or if symptoms recur
Symptoms improve in 2-3 weeks, full normalization takes 4-6 months
Weight loss typically 5-10% of gained weight after treatment initiation
Lipid panel will improve with thyroid replacement
Lifelong treatment required
pitfalls: Subclinical hypothyroidism (TSH 4.5-10, normal T4): treat if symptomatic, pregnant, TPO+, or TSH >10
Elderly or cardiac disease: start low (25-50 mcg daily), increase slowly (risk of angina, arrhythmias)
Drug interactions: levothyroxine absorption decreased by iron, calcium, PPIs - separate by 4 hours
Myxedema coma: severe hypothyroidism with altered mental status, hypothermia, hypoventilation → ICU, IV T3/T4, hydrocortisone
Central hypothyroidism: low TSH with low T4 (pituitary/hypothalamic disease) - different management

cases.title: Young Woman with Recurrent UTIs
learning_objectives: Recognize recurrent UTI patterns in women
Manage behavioral and pharmacologic prevention strategies
cases.presentation: 26-year-old woman with 5th UTI in past year, dysuria and frequency for 1 day

history.chief_complaint: Burning with urination, urinating every 30 minutes
history.hpi: Sudden onset dysuria yesterday, urinary frequency and urgency. Small amounts of urine each time. Lower abdominal discomfort. No fever, no back pain, no hematuria. Fifth UTI in 12 months, previously treated with nitrofurantoin with good response. Symptoms always occur 1-2 days after sexual intercourse. Uses diaphragm for contraception. Voids after intercourse 'sometimes.' Drinks 2-3 glasses water daily.
history.social: Sexually active with one partner, uses diaphragm and spermicide

physical_exam.abdomen: Suprapubic tenderness, no CVA tenderness
physical_exam.pelvic: Normal external genitalia, no vaginal discharge, no cervical motion tenderness

labs.urinalysis: Positive leukocyte esterase, positive nitrites, WBC >100/hpf, few bacteria
labs.urine_culture: Pending, previous cultures showed E. coli sensitive to all antibiotics

imaging.none_needed: Not indicated for uncomplicated recurrent UTI in young woman

differential: Interstitial cystitis (but acute onset, positive UA, response to antibiotics)
Pyelonephritis (but no fever, no CVA tenderness)
STI (urethritis/cervicitis - but no discharge, negative pelvic exam)
cases.explanation: Recurrent UTI defined as ≥2 infections in 6 months or ≥3 in 12 months. Almost always reinfection (new infection) rather than relapse (same organism). Risk factors: sexual activity, spermicide/diaphragm use, delayed post-coital voiding, low fluid intake, genetic susceptibility. E. coli causes 80% of UTIs. Spermicide alters vaginal flora, reducing lactobacilli that normally prevent pathogen colonization. Diaphragm can obstruct complete bladder emptying.
management_pearls: Acute treatment: Nitrofurantoin 100mg BID x 5 days (first-line for uncomplicated cystitis)
Behavioral modifications: Post-coital voiding within 15 minutes, increase fluid intake to 2-3L daily, avoid spermicide
Contraception change: Switch from diaphragm/spermicide to non-spermicidal method (OCPs, IUD, condoms without spermicide)
Prophylaxis indications: ≥2 UTIs in 6 months affecting quality of life
Prophylaxis options: (1) Post-coital single dose (nitrofurantoin 50-100mg or TMP-SMX SS), OR (2) Daily prophylaxis (nitrofurantoin 50mg qHS x 6-12 months)
Non-antibiotic prophylaxis: Cranberry supplements (36mg PACs daily), vaginal estrogen if postmenopausal, D-mannose
No imaging needed unless: pyelonephritis, hematuria, suspected anatomic abnormality
pitfalls: Complicated UTI: pregnancy, male, catheter, recent instrumentation, anatomic abnormality, immunosuppression → needs culture, longer treatment, possible imaging
Asymptomatic bacteriuria: positive culture without symptoms → do NOT treat (except pregnancy, pre-urologic procedure)
Pyelonephritis: fever, CVA tenderness, nausea → needs culture, 7-14 day treatment, consider admission
Antibiotic resistance: increasing fluoroquinolone and TMP-SMX resistance → culture-guided therapy if recurrent
Renal ultrasound/CT indicated if: recurrent pyelonephritis, hematuria, history of stones, suspected obstruction

cases.title: Knee Pain and Swelling After Fall
learning_objectives: Perform and interpret Lachman and anterior drawer tests
Understand Ottawa knee rules for imaging
cases.presentation: 22-year-old basketball player with acute knee pain, swelling, and instability after pivoting injury

history.chief_complaint: Left knee pain and swelling, feels unstable
history.hpi: Playing basketball yesterday, planted left foot and pivoted, felt sudden 'pop' in knee with immediate severe pain. Fell to ground, unable to continue playing. Significant swelling developed within 2-3 hours. Knee feels unstable, like it will 'give out.' Difficulty bearing weight. Iced overnight with minimal relief. No previous knee injuries.
history.social: College student, plays basketball recreationally 3x/week

physical_exam.left_knee: Moderate effusion, limited ROM due to pain and swelling. Full extension limited by 10 degrees. Tenderness along joint line. Positive Lachman test (soft endpoint, increased anterior translation). Positive anterior drawer. Negative posterior drawer. Negative varus/valgus stress. No patellar apprehension. Negative McMurray test.
physical_exam.neurovascular: Intact distal pulses, normal sensation, able to wiggle toes

imaging.knee_xray: No fracture, no dislocation. Large joint effusion.
imaging.mri_knee: Recommended for ligamentous evaluation - will show complete ACL tear

differential: Meniscus tear (joint line tenderness, positive McMurray, but less acute onset)
PCL tear (posterior drawer positive, dashboard injury mechanism)
MCL/LCL tear (valgus/varus stress positive, different mechanism)
Patellar dislocation (apprehension test positive, lateral displacement)
Tibial plateau fracture (usually older patients, more trauma, visible on XR)
cases.explanation: ACL (anterior cruciate ligament) tear is common sports injury, especially basketball, soccer, skiing. Mechanism: non-contact deceleration with pivoting/cutting, or direct blow to lateral knee. Classic presentation: audible 'pop,' immediate pain and swelling (hemarthrosis develops <2-4 hours), sense of instability. Physical exam: positive Lachman (most sensitive) and anterior drawer tests show increased anterior tibial translation. May have associated meniscal or collateral ligament injuries ('terrible triad' = ACL + MCL + medial meniscus).
management_pearls: Acute management: RICE (rest, ice, compression, elevation), crutches for comfort, NSAIDs
MRI to confirm diagnosis and assess for associated injuries (meniscus, other ligaments, bone bruising)
Arthrocentesis if tense effusion causing severe pain (often shows hemarthrosis)
Orthopedic referral within 1-2 weeks for surgical consultation
Surgical reconstruction: indicated for young, active patients, athletes. ACL reconstruction using patellar tendon or hamstring autograft.
Non-operative management: older, sedentary patients, or those unwilling to undergo surgery. Physical therapy for quadriceps strengthening, functional bracing.
Timeline: Surgery typically 2-4 weeks after injury (allow swelling to resolve, regain ROM), return to sports 6-9 months post-op
pitfalls: Missed posterior knee dislocation: check pulses, consider ABI, MR angiography if vascular injury suspected
Segond fracture (avulsion of lateral tibial plateau): pathognomonic for ACL tear on XR
Associated meniscal tears in 50%: clicking, locking, joint line tenderness
Pediatric ACL tears: physeal injuries possible, modified surgical techniques to avoid growth plate damage
Chronic ACL deficiency: recurrent instability, early-onset osteoarthritis, may develop secondary meniscal tears

cases.title: Severe Sore Throat with Exudates
learning_objectives: Use Centor criteria to assess strep throat probability
Understand appropriate testing and treatment strategies
Recognize complications of untreated strep pharyngitis
cases.presentation: 18-year-old with severe sore throat, fever, and tonsillar exudates for 2 days

history.chief_complaint: Worst sore throat of my life, can barely swallow
history.hpi: Sudden onset severe sore throat 2 days ago, fever to 102.5°F at home. Pain with swallowing, even liquids. No cough, no runny nose, no hoarseness. Noticed white patches on tonsils. Tender neck glands. Took ibuprofen with minimal relief. Several classmates have similar illness. No recent sick contacts outside school.
history.social: High school senior, no smoking, no alcohol

physical_exam.oropharynx: Markedly erythematous pharynx, enlarged tonsils with white exudates bilaterally, palatal petechiae. No uvular deviation. No trismus.
physical_exam.lymph_nodes: Tender, enlarged anterior cervical lymphadenopathy bilaterally
physical_exam.general: Ill-appearing, difficulty speaking due to pain

labs.throat_culture: Confirmatory if rapid test negative (not needed here)

imaging.none_needed: Clinical diagnosis with positive rapid strep

differential: Viral pharyngitis (but exudates, no cough, positive rapid strep support bacterial)
Infectious mononucleosis (Epstein-Barr) - exudates, fatigue, but negative rapid strep, heterophile positive
Peritonsillar abscess (unilateral, uvular deviation, trismus, muffled voice)
Epiglottitis (rare, drooling, stridor, tripod position - emergency)
cases.explanation: Strep pharyngitis caused by Group A Streptococcus (GAS, S. pyogenes). Accounts for 20-30% of pediatric, 5-15% of adult pharyngitis. Centor criteria: (1) Tonsillar exudates, (2) Tender anterior cervical adenopathy, (3) Fever, (4) Absence of cough. Score ≥3 → test for strep (rapid antigen or culture). Complications if untreated: acute rheumatic fever (rare in US), post-strep glomerulonephritis, peritonsillar abscess, toxic shock syndrome. Antibiotics shorten duration, reduce transmission, prevent complications.
management_pearls: First-line: Penicillin VK 500mg TID x 10 days OR amoxicillin 500mg TID x 10 days (better taste, once-daily dosing option)
Penicillin allergy: Azithromycin 500mg day 1, then 250mg days 2-5 (total 5 days) OR cephalexin (if no anaphylaxis to penicillin)
Pain control: NSAIDs (ibuprofen 400-600mg q6h), acetaminophen, salt water gargles, throat lozenges
Supportive: hydration, soft foods, rest
Contagious: avoid school/work for 24 hours after starting antibiotics
Follow-up: if no improvement in 48-72 hours (consider resistant organism, viral etiology, or complication)
No routine test of cure needed
pitfalls: Peritonsillar abscess: unilateral tonsillar swelling, uvular deviation, trismus, 'hot potato' voice → needs CT, ENT drainage
Infectious mononucleosis: avoid amoxicillin (causes rash in 90%), check monospot, manage supportively, no contact sports x 4 weeks (splenomegaly risk)
Scarlet fever: sandpaper rash, strawberry tongue - same organism (GAS), treat as strep throat
Fusobacterium necrophorum (Lemierre syndrome): severe pharyngitis, lateral neck pain, septic thrombophlebitis → rare but life-threatening
Antibiotic resistance: increasing macrolide resistance in some areas, consider if treatment failure

cases.title: Crushing Chest Pain Radiating to Jaw
learning_objectives: Interpret ECG findings of acute MI
cases.presentation: 62-year-old man with sudden onset crushing substernal chest pain radiating to jaw and left arm for 45 minutes

history.chief_complaint: Severe chest pain, pressure-like, radiating to jaw
history.hpi: Sudden onset severe substernal chest pressure while shoveling snow 45 minutes ago. 9/10 severity, crushing quality, radiating to jaw and left arm. Associated diaphoresis, nausea, shortness of breath. No relief with rest. No prior episodes. Had mild indigestion-like symptoms occasionally over past week.
history.pmh: Hypertension, hyperlipidemia, type 2 diabetes, 40 pack-year smoking history
history.medications: Lisinopril 40mg daily, atorvastatin 40mg daily, metformin 1000mg BID, aspirin 81mg daily
history.social: Current smoker (1 PPD), sedentary lifestyle

physical_exam.vitals: Temp 98.4°F, HR 102, BP 168/96, RR 22, O2 sat 94% on RA
physical_exam.cardiovascular: Tachycardia, regular rhythm, no murmurs, distant S4 gallop

labs.troponin_i: 0.8 ng/mL (elevated, will rise further at 6-12 hours)

imaging.ekg: ST-elevation 3-4mm in leads II, III, aVF (inferior STEMI). Reciprocal ST depression in I, aVL. Q waves forming in III, aVF.
imaging.echo: Will show inferior wall hypokinesis, reduced EF ~40%

differential: Aortic dissection (can have MI if dissection involves coronary ostia - need CTA if suspected)
Pulmonary embolism (dyspnea, but chest pain quality different, ECG shows ST elevation)
Pericarditis (ST elevation diffuse, concave upward, PR depression)
cases.explanation: ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) is complete coronary artery occlusion causing transmural myocardial necrosis. Inferior STEMI typically from right coronary artery occlusion. Classic presentation: crushing substernal chest pressure >20 minutes, radiation to jaw/arm, diaphoresis, dyspnea, nausea. Risk factors: smoking, hypertension, diabetes, hyperlipidemia, family history. ECG criteria: ST elevation ≥1mm in ≥2 contiguous leads. TIME IS MUSCLE - every minute delays increases myocardial necrosis and mortality.
management_pearls: IMMEDIATE: Call STEMI alert, activate cath lab, target door-to-balloon <90 minutes
Aspirin 324mg chew immediately (if not already given by EMS)
Dual antiplatelet: Ticagrelor 180mg load OR prasugrel 60mg OR clopidogrel 600mg
Anticoagulation: Heparin bolus + infusion
Nitrates: sublingual NTG 0.4mg q5min x3 if BP adequate (avoid if RV infarct - check right-sided ECG)
Morphine: 2-4mg IV for pain/anxiety (use sparingly, associated with worse outcomes)
Beta-blocker: metoprolol 5mg IV q5min x3 if no contraindications (HF, hypotension, bradycardia)
Primary PCI (percutaneous coronary intervention): preferred if <120 min, stent placement and restore flow
Fibrinolysis: if PCI not available within 120 min and <12 hours from symptom onset (tPA, TNK)
pitfalls: Right ventricular infarct: common with inferior MI, hypotension with nitrates/diuretics → give IV fluids, avoid preload reduction
Complete heart block: inferior MI can cause AV node ischemia → may need temporary pacing
Reperfusion arrhythmias: accelerated idioventricular rhythm (AIVR) after successful reperfusion - usually benign
Mechanical complications: papillary muscle rupture (acute MR), ventricular septal rupture, free wall rupture → days 3-7 post-MI
Post-MI care: dual antiplatelet x 12 months, high-intensity statin, beta-blocker, ACE inhibitor, cardiac rehab

cases.title: Sudden Onset Severe Headache
learning_objectives: Recognize thunderclap headache as red flag
Interpret non-contrast CT and LP findings
cases.presentation: 48-year-old with sudden, severe 'worst headache of life' while exercising, peak intensity within seconds

history.chief_complaint: Sudden, explosive headache - worst ever
history.hpi: At gym doing weightlifting 2 hours ago, sudden onset of severe headache - 'like thunderclap,' reached maximum intensity within seconds. 10/10 severity, diffuse but worse occipitally. Associated nausea, vomited twice. Brief loss of consciousness witnessed (~10 seconds). Photophobia, neck stiffness. Never had headache like this. No recent trauma. No fever.
history.social: Non-smoker, occasional alcohol, works as attorney (high stress)

physical_exam.neurologic: Alert but uncomfortable. Cranial nerves intact. No focal deficits. Nuchal rigidity present. Positive Kernig's sign. Photophobia. Normal fundoscopy (no papilledema).

imaging.ct_head_non_contrast: Hyperdensity in basal cisterns and Sylvian fissures consistent with subarachnoid blood. No hydrocephalus. No mass effect.
imaging.cta_head: Shows 7mm aneurysm at anterior communicating artery
imaging.lumbar_puncture: Not needed if SAH visible on CT; if CT negative and high suspicion → LP shows xanthochromia, elevated RBCs

differential: Reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome (RCVS) - similar presentation, negative imaging initially
Meningitis (but sudden onset, brief LOC, CT findings favor SAH)
Migraine (but thunderclap onset, syncope, meningismus atypical)
Cervical artery dissection (neck pain, Horner's syndrome)
cases.explanation: Subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) is bleeding into subarachnoid space, most commonly from ruptured cerebral aneurysm (85% of non-traumatic SAH). Classic presentation: sudden, severe 'thunderclap' headache reaching peak intensity within seconds-minutes, often described as 'worst headache of life.' Associated features: nausea/vomiting, photophobia, nuchal rigidity, brief loss of consciousness (sentinel bleed in 50% days-weeks prior). Risk factors: HTN, smoking, family history, polycystic kidney disease. HIGH MORTALITY (~50%) - urgent diagnosis and treatment critical.
management_pearls: IMMEDIATE: Non-contrast head CT (98% sensitive if done <6 hours), if negative and high suspicion → LP for xanthochromia/RBCs
CT angiography (CTA) to identify aneurysm location and size
Urgent neurosurgery consultation for aneurysm securing (surgical clipping vs endovascular coiling)
ICU admission: neuro checks q1h, strict BP control (SBP <160 mmHg, avoid hypotension), seizure prophylaxis (levetiracetam)
Nimodipine 60mg PO/NG q4h x 21 days (prevents vasospasm, improves outcomes)
Monitor for complications: rebleeding (highest risk first 24h), vasospasm (days 3-14), hydrocephalus
Serial transcranial Dopplers to detect vasospasm
NPO until aneurysm secured (cough/strain increases ICP)
pitfalls: Sentinel headache: 50% have warning leak days-weeks prior - any sudden severe headache needs workup
CT sensitivity decreases with time: 93% at 24h, <50% at 1 week - LP essential if CT negative and high suspicion
Lumbar puncture: xanthochromia (CSF yellow from bilirubin) is key - present after RBCs have lysed, peaks 12h-2 weeks

Vasospasm: delayed complication days 3-14, presents with focal deficits or decreased consciousness - 'triple-H therapy' (hypertension, hypervolemia, hemodilution) controversial, nimodipine proven benefit
Hydrocephalus: can be acute (obstructive) or delayed (communicating) - may need EVD or VP shunt

cases.title: Elderly Woman with Hip Pain After Fall
learning_objectives: Understand imaging approach and fracture types
cases.presentation: 82-year-old woman with right hip pain and inability to bear weight after fall at home

history.chief_complaint: Right hip pain, can't walk after fall
history.hpi: Fell in bathroom last night while getting up from toilet. Landed on right side. Immediate severe right hip pain, unable to stand or bear weight. Called daughter who brought her to ED this morning. Denies loss of consciousness, no head trauma. Right leg appears shorter. Pain 8/10, worse with any movement.
history.pmh: Osteoporosis (not on treatment), hypertension, hypothyroidism, history of previous wrist fracture
history.medications: Lisinopril 10mg daily, levothyroxine 75mcg daily, aspirin 81mg daily
history.social: Lives alone (widowed), independent with ADLs, uses cane for ambulation
history.family: Mother had hip fracture at age 80

physical_exam.right_lower_extremity: Right leg shortened, externally rotated at rest. Severe pain with log roll. No open wounds. Tenderness over right hip. Unable to perform straight leg raise.
physical_exam.neurovascular: Distal pulses intact, normal sensation, can wiggle toes
physical_exam.general: Elderly woman in pain, holding right leg still

imaging.hip_xray: Intertrochanteric fracture of right femur with displacement. No femoral neck fracture.

differential: Femoral neck fracture (intracapsular, higher AVN risk)
Subtrochanteric fracture (below lesser trochanter, different fixation)
Pubic rami fracture (less severe, often managed non-operatively)
cases.explanation: Hip fractures in elderly are major cause of morbidity/mortality. Two main types: (1) Femoral neck (intracapsular) - higher risk AVN due to disrupted blood supply, often needs hemiarthroplasty; (2) Intertrochanteric (extracapsular) - better blood supply, managed with ORIF (intramedullary nail or sliding hip screw). Classic presentation: fall, inability to bear weight, shortened and externally rotated leg. Risk factors: osteoporosis, age >65, female, previous fracture, vitamin D deficiency. 1-year mortality 20-30%.
management_pearls: Pain control: multimodal analgesia (acetaminophen, opioids PRN, nerve block - fascia iliaca or femoral nerve block)
NPO after midnight for surgery, IV fluids
Orthopedic consultation: surgical repair within 24-48 hours reduces mortality and complications
Surgical treatment: intramedullary nail (cephalomedullary nail) preferred for intertrochanteric fractures - allows early weight bearing
DVT prophylaxis: LMWH (enoxaparin) or fondaparinux starting 6-12h post-op
Early mobilization: PT/OT starting post-op day 1, progressive weight bearing as tolerated
Osteoporosis treatment: start bisphosphonate (alendronate) or denosumab, calcium 1200mg + vitamin D 800-1000 IU daily
Discharge planning: most need rehab facility, assess home safety, fall prevention
pitfalls: Occult fracture: 3-10% of hip fractures not visible on initial XR - if high suspicion and negative XR → get MRI (most sensitive)
Surgical delay >48h: associated with increased mortality, pressure ulcers, pneumonia, delirium
Post-op complications: delirium (25-50%), DVT/PE, MI, pneumonia, UTI, pressure ulcers
Bisphosphonate timing: controversial if started immediately vs delayed - some start 2 weeks post-op to avoid impaired fracture healing
Non-operative management: only if patient non-ambulatory at baseline or severe medical comorbidities preclude surgery - associated with worse outcomes

cases.title: Productive Cough with Fever and Chest Pain
learning_objectives: Apply CURB-65 criteria for severity assessment
cases.presentation: 68-year-old with productive cough, fever, and right-sided pleuritic chest pain for 3 days

history.chief_complaint: Cough with yellow sputum, fever, right chest pain
history.hpi: Gradual onset of cough 5 days ago, initially dry, now productive of yellow-green sputum. Fever to 102.8°F at home. Developed sharp right-sided chest pain 2 days ago, worse with deep breathing and coughing. Shortness of breath with exertion. Chills, no hemoptysis. Taking OTC cold medicine with no improvement. Increased confusion noted by daughter today.
history.pmh: COPD (on inhalers), hypertension, diabetes type 2, prior pneumonia 2 years ago
history.medications: Tiotropium inhaler daily, albuterol PRN, lisinopril 20mg, metformin 1000mg BID
history.social: Former smoker (quit 5 years ago, 40 pack-year history), lives with daughter

physical_exam.vitals: Temp 101.6°F, HR 102, BP 108/68, RR 26, O2 sat 89% on RA
physical_exam.general: Elderly man in moderate respiratory distress, appears ill
physical_exam.lungs: Decreased breath sounds right lower lobe, bronchial breath sounds, egophony, dullness to percussion RLL. Coarse crackles right base.
physical_exam.mental_status: Oriented to person and place, confused about date

labs.bmp: Na 133 mEq/L, creatinine 1.4 mg/dL, BUN 32 mg/dL

imaging.chest_xray: Right lower lobe consolidation, no effusion, no pneumothorax

differential: Aspiration pneumonia (RLL common site, risk factors present)
COPD exacerbation (but infiltrate present, fever, elevated WBC)
Pulmonary embolism (pleuritic pain, dyspnea, but consolidation present)
Lung abscess (indolent, foul-smelling sputum, cavitation on imaging)
Tuberculosis (chronic cough, weight loss, upper lobe cavitary lesions)
cases.explanation: Community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) is acute infection of lung parenchyma acquired outside hospital. Common pathogens: S. pneumoniae (most common), H. influenzae, atypical organisms (Mycoplasma, Chlamydia, Legionella). Classic lobar pneumonia: fever, productive cough, pleuritic chest pain, dyspnea. Physical exam: focal consolidation (bronchial breath sounds, egophony, dullness), crackles. CURB-65 score determines severity: Confusion, Urea >20 mg/dL, RR ≥30, BP <90/60, age ≥65. This patient: CURB-65 = 4 (confusion, BUN >20, RR ≥30, age ≥65) → high risk, needs hospital admission.
management_pearls: Severity assessment: CURB-65 score 0-1 outpatient, 2 consider admission, ≥3 hospitalize (ICU if ≥4)
Empiric antibiotics (inpatient): Ceftriaxone 1g IV daily + azithromycin 500mg IV daily (covers typical + atypical)
Alternative: respiratory fluoroquinolone (levofloxacin 750mg IV daily) - monotherapy adequate
Oxygen supplementation to maintain sat >90%
IV fluids for sepsis/dehydration
Blood and sputum cultures before antibiotics (don't delay treatment)
Follow-up CXR in 6 weeks to ensure resolution (rule out underlying malignancy in elderly smokers)
Duration: 5 days if afebrile 48-72h and clinically stable, longer if slow response or bacteremia
pitfalls: Healthcare-associated pneumonia (HCAP): recent hospitalization, nursing home, dialysis, antibiotics within 90 days → higher MRSA/Pseudomonas risk, broader coverage needed
Aspiration pneumonia: RLL common, witnessed aspiration, poor dentition → add anaerobic coverage (ampicillin-sulbactam or clindamycin)
Empyema: parapneumonic effusion with positive culture, needs thoracentesis/chest tube
Septic shock: hypotension, lactate >2 → needs ICU, vasopressors, 30 mL/kg IV bolus
Non-resolving pneumonia: persistent symptoms/infiltrate at 72h → consider resistant organism, empyema, obstruction, immunocompromised, incorrect diagnosis

cases.title: Jaundice and Right Upper Quadrant Pain
learning_objectives: Interpret liver function tests and bilirubin patterns
Understand role of imaging in biliary disease
cases.presentation: 58-year-old with yellowing eyes, dark urine, and RUQ pain for 2 days

history.chief_complaint: Yellow eyes, dark urine, right upper belly pain
history.hpi: Developed colicky RUQ pain 2 days ago, initially intermittent, now constant. Pain radiates to right shoulder. Nausea, multiple episodes vomiting, no relief after vomiting. Yesterday noticed eyes looked yellow, urine very dark (tea-colored), stools lighter than usual. Fever to 101.2°F at home. Similar but milder RUQ pain episodes in past after fatty meals.
history.pmh: Obesity (BMI 38), diabetes type 2, hypertension, prior gallstones on ultrasound 1 year ago (asymptomatic, no treatment)
history.social: Denies alcohol, no drugs, works as chef

physical_exam.abdomen: RUQ tenderness, positive Murphy's sign (inspiratory arrest with palpation of RUQ). No rebound or guarding. No masses. Bowel sounds present.

labs.lfts: AST 210 U/L, ALT 245 U/L, Alk Phos 380 U/L, Total bili 6.8 mg/dL (direct 5.2 mg/dL)

imaging.ruq_ultrasound: Gallbladder wall thickening, pericholecystic fluid, gallstones present. Common bile duct dilated at 9mm with echogenic focus suggesting stone. No intrahepatic ductal dilation.
imaging.mrcp: Confirmatory imaging - shows CBD stone, dilated CBD

differential: Acute cholecystitis (RUQ pain, fever, but jaundice suggests CBD obstruction)
Ascending cholangitis (this patient has Charcot triad - fever, jaundice, RUQ pain)
Hepatitis (elevated transaminases, but cholestatic pattern, imaging findings favor biliary obstruction)
Pancreatic cancer (painless jaundice, but acute onset, stones on imaging)
Acute pancreatitis (but lipase normal, ultrasound shows biliary pathology)
cases.explanation: Choledocholithiasis is gallstone in common bile duct causing obstruction. Presents with Charcot triad: fever, jaundice, RUQ pain (ascending cholangitis). Labs show cholestatic pattern: elevated direct bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, mild transaminase elevation. CBD stone causes biliary obstruction → bacterial ascending infection. Risk factors: gallstones (15% migrate to CBD), obesity, female, forty, fertile (4 F's). If untreated progresses to septic shock (Reynolds pentad: Charcot triad + altered mental status + hypotension).
management_pearls: NPO, IV fluids, pain control (avoid morphine - causes sphincter of Oddi spasm)
Broad-spectrum IV antibiotics: Piperacillin-tazobactam 3.375g q6h OR ceftriaxone 1g daily + metronidazole 500mg q8h
Blood cultures before antibiotics
Urgent ERCP (endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography) for stone extraction and stenting within 24-48 hours
Surgery consultation for cholecystectomy (after ERCP, once stabilized - within same hospitalization if possible)
Monitor for sepsis: if hypotension or altered mental status → ICU, vasopressors, emergent ERCP/biliary drainage
Post-ERCP: check for pancreatitis (elevated lipase), perforation, bleeding
pitfalls: Reynolds pentad: Charcot triad + confusion + hypotension = severe cholangitis, needs emergent biliary decompression
ERCP complications: pancreatitis (5%), bleeding, perforation, infection
Mirizzi syndrome: gallstone in cystic duct/GB neck compresses CBD causing obstruction - ERCP may not resolve, needs surgery
Cholangiocarcinoma: painless jaundice in elderly, weight loss, imaging shows mass - needs ERCP with biopsy
Primary sclerosing cholangitis: chronic biliary inflammation, associated with IBD, MRCP shows strictures

cases.title: Difficulty Swallowing Solid Foods
learning_objectives: Understand role of endoscopy in dysphagia evaluation
cases.presentation: 52-year-old with progressive difficulty swallowing solid foods and sensation of food getting stuck for 3 months

history.chief_complaint: Food getting stuck in chest, difficulty swallowing solids
history.hpi: Progressive difficulty swallowing over 3 months, initially only with meat/bread, now any solid food. Sensation of food getting stuck mid-chest, requires water to wash it down. Occasionally regurgitates undigested food. No difficulty with liquids. Eating smaller bites, avoiding certain foods. 12-pound weight loss. Longstanding heartburn symptoms, takes Tums daily. No odynophagia (painful swallowing). No hematemesis.
history.social: Non-smoker, occasional alcohol, works as teacher

physical_exam.vitals: Temp 98.6°F, HR 72, BP 124/78, RR 14, Weight 168 lbs (was 180 lbs 3 months ago)
physical_exam.abdomen: Soft, non-tender, no masses

imaging.barium_swallow: Shows narrowing of distal esophagus with bird-beak appearance, delayed emptying
imaging.egd: Recommended - likely shows esophageal stricture or eosinophilic esophagitis

differential: Esophageal stricture from GERD (chronic reflux causing scarring)
Esophageal cancer (weight loss, progressive dysphagia - needs EGD to rule out)
Achalasia (dysphagia to solids AND liquids, bird-beak on barium swallow)
Schatzki ring (intermittent dysphagia with solids, especially meat)
cases.explanation: Eosinophilic esophagitis (EoE) is chronic immune-mediated esophageal disease characterized by eosinophil infiltration. Presents with progressive solid food dysphagia, food impaction episodes, history of atopy/allergies common. Pathophysiology: food allergens trigger eosinophilic inflammation → esophageal remodeling and stricture formation. More common in young males. Associated with other allergic conditions (asthma, allergic rhinitis, food allergies). EGD shows rings/furrows ('corrugated' or 'feline' esophagus), white exudates, strictures. Diagnosis: ≥15 eosinophils per high-power field on esophageal biopsy.
management_pearls: EGD with biopsies (at least 6 samples from proximal, mid, distal esophagus) - diagnostic gold standard
PPI trial: Start high-dose PPI (omeprazole 40mg BID) x 8 weeks - treats GERD and has anti-eosinophilic effects
Topical steroids: Fluticasone MDI 880 mcg BID (swallowed, not inhaled) OR budesonide 1mg oral viscous slurry BID
Dietary elimination: Six-food elimination diet (dairy, wheat, egg, soy, nuts, seafood) - effective but difficult
Esophageal dilation: if stricture present causing dysphagia - higher perforation risk than in other conditions, use caution
Food impaction: emergent EGD for disimpaction if unable to swallow secretions
Monitor: repeat EGD with biopsies after 8-12 weeks of treatment to assess response
pitfalls: Esophageal cancer: must rule out with EGD/biopsy, especially age >50, weight loss, smoking history
Achalasia: dysphagia to both solids AND liquids, regurgitation, bird-beak on esophagram - needs manometry for diagnosis
Food impaction: most common complication of EoE - avoid enzymes (papain/meat tenderizer), use glucagon 1mg IV or emergent EGD
Stricture dilation complications: higher perforation risk (up to 0.3%) compared to peptic strictures
GERD vs EoE: 30% respond to PPI alone (PPI-responsive esophageal eosinophilia), may have overlapping features

cases.title: Muscle Weakness and Difficulty Rising from Chair
learning_objectives: Interpret muscle enzymes and EMG findings
cases.presentation: 54-year-old woman with progressive proximal muscle weakness, difficulty climbing stairs and standing from seated position for 2 months

history.chief_complaint: Weakness in arms and legs, hard to get up from chair
history.hpi: Progressive weakness over 2 months, initially noticed difficulty brushing hair (arms tired quickly), now trouble climbing stairs, rising from chair without using arms. Muscle soreness/achiness. Fatigue. No sensory changes, no vision changes. Noticed dark purple rash on eyelids last month. No dysphagia, no dyspnea. Lost 8 pounds (unintentional).
history.social: Non-smoker, no alcohol, works as accountant

physical_exam.musculoskeletal: Proximal muscle weakness: shoulder abduction 3/5, hip flexion 3/5. Distal strength normal (4+/5). Unable to rise from chair without using arms. Difficulty lifting arms above head. Muscle tenderness present.
physical_exam.skin: Violaceous (heliotrope) rash on eyelids, erythematous papules over knuckles (Gottron papules)
physical_exam.neurologic: Normal sensation, reflexes 2+ and symmetric, cranial nerves intact

imaging.mri_thigh: T2 signal hyperintensity in proximal thigh muscles consistent with edema/inflammation
imaging.emg: Shows myopathic pattern - short duration, low amplitude polyphasic motor units, early recruitment
imaging.chest_ct: Mild interstitial changes, no mass (malignancy screening)

differential: Inclusion body myositis (distal AND proximal weakness, older age, slower progression)
Statin-induced myopathy (but not on statins, CPK usually <10x normal)
Hypothyroid myopathy (but TSH normal, lower CPK elevation)
Muscular dystrophy (chronic, family history, different pattern)
cases.explanation: Dermatomyositis is autoimmune inflammatory myopathy causing proximal muscle weakness and characteristic skin findings. Classic rash: heliotrope (violaceous periorbital), Gottron papules (erythematous papules over knuckles/joints), shawl sign, V-sign. Muscle involvement: symmetric proximal weakness (difficulty rising from chair, climbing stairs, lifting arms). Labs: markedly elevated CPK (often >1000), positive ANA, myositis-specific antibodies (MSAs). EMG shows myopathic pattern. MRI shows muscle edema. Muscle biopsy confirms diagnosis. Associated with malignancy in 15-25% (ovarian, lung, colorectal, pancreatic) - requires age-appropriate cancer screening.
management_pearls: Rheumatology referral urgently for confirmation and treatment initiation
Muscle biopsy: confirmatory - shows perivascular/perimysicular inflammation, perifascicular atrophy
Malignancy screening: age-appropriate (mammogram, colonoscopy, Pap smear, CT chest/abdomen/pelvis)
Corticosteroids: Prednisone 1mg/kg/day (typically 60-80mg daily) as first-line - expect CPK improvement in 4-6 weeks, strength in 3-6 months
Steroid-sparing agents: Methotrexate 15-25mg weekly OR azathioprine 2mg/kg/day (added early to allow steroid taper)
Severe/refractory: IVIG 2g/kg monthly, rituximab, mycophenolate
Physical therapy: once inflammation controlled, progressive strengthening
Interstitial lung disease screening: PFTs, chest HRCT - present in 30-40%
pitfalls: Malignancy association: perform comprehensive cancer screening, particularly in patients >40 years old
Interstitial lung disease: can be presenting feature, rapidly progressive - needs PFTs, HRCT, may need aggressive immunosuppression
Steroid myopathy: chronic steroid use can worsen weakness despite controlled inflammation - monitor CPK
Inclusion body myositis: often misdiagnosed as polymyositis, but distal weakness, poor steroid response, quadriceps atrophy
Dysphagia/aspiration: 30-50% develop esophageal dysmotility, may need modified barium swallow
Cardiac involvement: rare but can cause heart block, myocarditis - baseline EKG, consider echo

cases.title: Child with Barking Cough and Stridor
learning_objectives: Recognize croup presentation and severity grading
Understand role of corticosteroids in croup
cases.presentation: 2-year-old with barking cough, hoarse voice, and noisy breathing for 2 days

history.chief_complaint: Barking cough, difficulty breathing
history.hpi: Started with runny nose and lowgrade fever 3 days ago. Last night developed distinctive barking/'seal-like' cough. This morning voice hoarse, breathing noisy (especially when inhaling). Worse tonight - parents heard high-pitched sound when breathing in. Cough worse at night. Still drinking fluids, no drooling. Playing but seems more tired. Previous URI 1 month ago resolved without issues.
history.pmh: Full-term birth, up-to-date immunizations including Hib
history.social: Daycare attendance, older sibling recently had cold

physical_exam.vitals: Temp 100.4°F, HR 135, RR 32, O2 sat 96% on RA
physical_exam.general: Alert toddler, mildly distressed, sitting in parent's lap
physical_exam.heent: Hoarse voice, no drooling. Oropharynx shows no obstruction, no trismus. Mildly erythematous throat.
physical_exam.lungs: Inspiratory stridor at rest, barking cough during exam. No wheezing. Mild subcostal retractions. Air entry adequate bilaterally.

imaging.neck_xray_lateral: Can show subglottic narrowing ('steeple sign') but not routinely needed
imaging.ap_neck_xray: Narrowing of subglottic trachea if obtained

differential: Epiglottitis (but no drooling, toxic appearance, stridor less prominent, can swallow - epiglottitis rare post-Hib vaccine)
Foreign body aspiration (sudden onset, unilateral findings, no viral prodrome)
Bacterial tracheitis (toxic appearance, high fever, purulent secretions)
Peritonsillar abscess (older child, trismus, uvular deviation)
Anaphylaxis (acute onset, urticaria, known allergen exposure)
cases.explanation: Croup (laryngotracheobronchitis) is viral infection causing subglottic inflammation and edema. Most common pathogen: parainfluenza virus. Peak age 6 months - 3 years. Classic presentation: prodromal URI → barking/seal-like cough, hoarse voice, inspiratory stridor (narrowed upper airway), worse at night. Severity grading: mild (occasional barking cough, no stridor at rest), moderate (stridor at rest, mild retractions), severe (severe stridor, significant retractions, agitation/lethargy). Usually self-limited, resolves in 3-7 days.
management_pearls: Dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg PO/IM x1 dose (max 16mg) - ALL patients, even mild croup (reduces ED visits, hospitalizations)
Nebulized epinephrine (racemic 0.5 mL of 2.25% solution in 3 mL NS): for moderate-severe croup with stridor at rest - provides rapid but temporary relief (observe 2-3 hours for rebound)
Humidified air: traditional but limited evidence, may provide comfort
Pulse oximetry monitoring if moderate-severe
Discharge if: mild croup, stridor resolves, tolerating PO, reliable caregivers
Admit if: severe croup, persistent stridor after epinephrine, hypoxia, poor oral intake, social concerns
Parents: expect cough to persist 3-7 days, return if worsening respiratory distress, unable to drink, drooling
pitfalls: Epiglottitis: toxic appearance, drooling, tripod positioning, muffled voice (vs hoarse) → EMERGENCY, do NOT examine throat, call anesthesia/ENT
Bacterial tracheitis: croup that worsens despite treatment, high fever, toxic appearance → needs airway management, antibiotics
Recurrent croup: consider subglottic stenosis, hemangioma, anatomic abnormality → ENT referral for laryngoscopy
Hypoxia: late finding in croup, indicates severe obstruction → needs epinephrine, possible intubation
Agitation: can worsen airway obstruction - avoid unnecessary procedures, keep child calm in parent's arms
