cases.title: Vaginal Discharge and Itching
learning_objectives: Differentiate BV from candidiasis and trichomoniasis
Understand pH and wet mount findings
cases.presentation: 32-year-old with malodorous vaginal discharge and mild itching for 1 week

history.chief_complaint: Vaginal discharge with fishy odor
history.hpi: Noticed thin, grayish-white vaginal discharge 1 week ago with unpleasant fishy odor, especially after intercourse. Mild vulvar itching, no burning with urination. No abdominal pain. Recently finished course of antibiotics for sinusitis. Sexually active with one male partner (monogamous). No new partners. Using condoms inconsistently. LMP 2 weeks ago (regular cycles).
history.pmh: No STI history, no previous vaginitis
history.social: Non-smoker, occasional alcohol

physical_exam.abdomen: Soft, non-tender
physical_exam.pelvic: Normal external genitalia, thin gray-white homogeneous discharge coating vaginal walls. No erythema. Cervix normal appearing, no cervical motion tenderness. Positive 'whiff test' (fishy odor with KOH).

labs.wet_mount: Clue cells present (epithelial cells studded with bacteria), few WBCs

differential: Vulvovaginal candidiasis (thick white cottage cheese discharge, pH normal, yeast on KOH)
Trichomoniasis (frothy yellow-green discharge, pH >4.5, motile trichomonads on wet mount)
Normal physiologic discharge (no odor, pH <4.5, lactobacilli predominant)
Cervicitis (mucopurulent discharge from cervix, cervical friability)
Atrophic vaginitis (postmenopausal, thin discharge, vaginal atrophy)
cases.explanation: Bacterial vaginosis (BV) is disruption of normal vaginal flora - overgrowth of anaerobic bacteria (Gardnerella vaginalis, Prevotella, Mobiluncus) replacing lactobacilli. Not an STI but associated with sexual activity. Amsel criteria (3 of 4 required): (1) Thin gray-white discharge, (2) pH >4.5, (3) Positive whiff test, (4) Clue cells on microscopy. Increased risk after antibiotics, douching, new sexual partners. Complications: increased STI risk, PID, pregnancy complications (preterm birth).
management_pearls: First-line: Metronidazole 500mg PO BID x 7 days OR metronidazole 0.75% gel intravaginally qHS x 5 days
Alternative: Clindamycin 300mg PO BID x 7 days OR clindamycin 2% cream intravaginally qHS x 7 days
Single-dose metronidazole 2g NOT recommended (higher failure rates)
Avoid alcohol during and 24-48h after metronidazole (disulfiram reaction)
No treatment needed for male partners (not sexually transmitted)
Pregnant women with BV: treat even if asymptomatic (reduces preterm birth risk)
Recurrent BV (≥3 in year): suppressive therapy - metronidazole gel 2x weekly x 4-6 months
pitfalls: Trichomoniasis: treat partner also (STI), use metronidazole 2g single dose or 500mg BID x 7 days
Candidiasis: usually thick white discharge, pH normal, intense pruritus → treat with fluconazole 150mg single dose or topical azole
Pregnancy: oral metronidazole safe in 2nd-3rd trimester; avoid clindamycin cream (increased preterm birth)
Recurrent BV: consider boric acid 600mg vaginal suppository daily x 14-21 days as alternative
Cervicitis: if cervical discharge/friability, test for gonorrhea/chlamydia, treat empirically

cases.title: Sudden Loss of Vision in One Eye
learning_objectives: Recognize central retinal artery occlusion as emergency
Understand time-critical nature of retinal ischemia
cases.presentation: 72-year-old with sudden, painless loss of vision in right eye 2 hours ago

history.chief_complaint: Can't see out of right eye, happened suddenly
history.hpi: Sudden, complete vision loss in right eye 2 hours ago while eating breakfast - 'like curtain came down.' No pain. No flashes, floaters, or trauma. Left eye vision normal. Brief episode of vision loss in same eye 3 days ago lasting ~5 minutes, then resolved. No headache, no jaw claudication, no scalp tenderness. No amaurosis in other eye.
history.pmh: Atrial fibrillation (not anticoagulated), hypertension, hyperlipidemia, CAD s/p MI 5 years ago, carotid stenosis 60% right ICA
history.social: Former smoker (quit 10 years ago), no alcohol

physical_exam.ophthalmologic: Right eye: no light perception, RAPD (relative afferent pupillary defect) present. Fundoscopy: pale, opaque retina with cherry-red spot at fovea, attenuated arterioles, boxcarring of blood in vessels. Left eye: 20/30 vision, normal fundoscopy.
physical_exam.cardiovascular: Irregularly irregular rhythm (AFib), carotid bruit right side

imaging.echocardiogram: Low EF 35%, no visible thrombus, moderate LA enlargement

differential: Retinal detachment (floaters, flashes, peripheral visual field loss first)
Vitreous hemorrhage (floaters, hazy red reflex, no cherry-red spot)
Ischemic optic neuropathy (pale optic disc, no cherry-red spot)
Giant cell arteritis (older, temporal artery tenderness, elevated ESR - EMERGENT)
Stroke (occipital lobe) - bilateral homonymous hemianopsia, not monocular
cases.explanation: Central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO) is ocular stroke - sudden occlusion of central retinal artery causing retinal ischemia. 'Eye attack' - retinal tissue tolerates ischemia <90-100 minutes before irreversible damage. Most common cause: embolism (carotid atherosclerosis, cardiac source - AFib, valve disease). Classic fundoscopy: pale/opaque retina (edema), cherry-red spot at fovea (choroidal circulation intact), attenuated arterioles, boxcarring (segmented blood column). RAPD present. Prior transient monocular vision loss (amaurosis fugax) = warning TIA.
management_pearls: OPHTHALMOLOGY EMERGENCY - immediate consultation, ideally within 90 minutes
Globe massage: 5-10 seconds firm pressure, release x multiple cycles (attempt to dislodge embolus)
Anterior chamber paracentesis: by ophthalmologist, removes aqueous to acutely lower IOP
Hyperbaric oxygen: if available within 24 hours, may salvage some vision
IV acetazolamide 500mg: lowers IOP
Lower head of bed flat: improve retinal perfusion
Workup for embolic source: carotid ultrasound, echocardiogram, telemetry for AFib
Start anticoagulation for AFib (if CRAO cardioembolic)
Prognosis: poor - most remain legally blind despite treatment due to late presentation
pitfalls: Giant cell arteritis (GCA): age >50, new headache, jaw claudication, elevated ESR → start prednisone 60mg IMMEDIATELY (prevent fellow eye involvement), temporal artery biopsy within 1-2 weeks
Time is retina: <90 min ischemia time for potential recovery - most patients present >6 hours (permanent vision loss)
Branch retinal artery occlusion: sectoral vision loss, better prognosis than CRAO
Cilioretinal artery: present in 15-30%, if spared may preserve central vision despite CRAO
Hyperacute treatment unproven: globe massage, paracentesis, hyperbaric oxygen have limited evidence but attempted due to devastating prognosis

cases.title: Joint Pain and Morning Stiffness
learning_objectives: Understand importance of early diagnosis and treatment
Interpret rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP antibodies
cases.presentation: 44-year-old woman with symmetric hand and wrist pain, morning stiffness >1 hour, for 4 months

history.chief_complaint: Swollen, painful hands, morning stiffness
history.hpi: Progressive hand and wrist pain over 4 months. Bilateral, symmetric involvement of MCP and PIP joints. Morning stiffness lasting 2-3 hours, improves with activity. Hands feel swollen, tight. Difficulty making fist, opening jars, buttoning shirts. Recently noticed feet also painful (MTP joints). Fatigue worsening. NSAIDs provide minimal relief. No skin rash, no eye symptoms. 8-pound weight loss.
history.social: Non-smoker, works as dental hygienist (hand-intensive work)

physical_exam.hands: Symmetric swelling and tenderness of bilateral MCP joints (2nd-4th), PIP joints. Decreased grip strength. No DIP involvement. Wrists with boggy synovitis, reduced ROM.
physical_exam.feet: Tenderness and swelling of bilateral MTP joints (squeeze test positive)

labs.cbc: Mild normocytic anemia (Hgb 11.2 g/dL), platelets normal

imaging.hand_xray: Soft tissue swelling around MCPs and PIPs, periarticular osteopenia. No erosions yet (early disease).

differential: Psoriatic arthritis (but no psoriasis, no DIP involvement, negative skin findings)
Systemic lupus erythematosus (but negative ANA, no systemic features)
Polymyalgia rheumatica (older, proximal muscles, no small joint involvement)
Osteoarthritis (DIP involvement common, no prolonged morning stiffness)
cases.explanation: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is chronic autoimmune inflammatory arthritis causing symmetric polyarthritis. Pathophysiology: autoantibodies (RF, anti-CCP) against joint synovium → chronic inflammation → joint destruction and erosions. Classic presentation: symmetric small joint involvement (MCP, PIP, wrists, MTPs), prolonged morning stiffness (>1 hour), improves with activity. Extra-articular: rheumatoid nodules, interstitial lung disease, vasculitis, Sjögren's. ACR/EULAR criteria for diagnosis. Anti-CCP highly specific (95%), predicts erosive disease. Early treatment critical - window of opportunity in first 3-6 months to prevent irreversible damage.
management_pearls: URGENT rheumatology referral - treat within 3 months of symptom onset (window of opportunity)
DMARD (disease-modifying antirheumatic drug) - start immediately: Methotrexate 15mg PO weekly (first-line), titrate to 20-25mg
Folic acid 1mg daily (reduce MTX side effects)
Prednisone bridge: 10-20mg daily x 4-6 weeks during DMARD onset (takes 6-12 weeks to work), then taper
Monitor: CBC, CMP q4-8 weeks on methotrexate (bone marrow suppression, hepatotoxicity)
If inadequate response: add or switch to biologic (TNF inhibitor - adalimumab, etanercept, OR JAK inhibitor - tofacitinib)
Treat-to-target: goal is remission or low disease activity, escalate therapy if not achieved
Pneumococcal and influenza vaccines before starting immunosuppression
pitfalls: Delay in diagnosis/treatment: each month of untreated RA increases erosion risk - refer urgently even if RF negative (seronegative RA in 20%)
Methotrexate contraindications: pregnancy (teratogenic - reliable contraception required), significant liver disease, excessive alcohol use
Biologic screening: TB (PPD or IGRA), hepatitis B/C before starting biologics
Interstitial lung disease: baseline CXR, consider PFTs - methotrexate can worsen, biologics may be safer
Drug monitoring: methotrexate can cause bone marrow suppression, hepatotoxicity - regular lab monitoring essential
Seronegative RA: 20% RF and anti-CCP negative - diagnosis based on clinical presentation, may have worse prognosis

cases.title: Painful Swollen Big Toe
learning_objectives: Understand role of synovial fluid analysis
cases.presentation: 58-year-old man with sudden onset severe pain and swelling of right great toe, woke him from sleep

history.chief_complaint: Severe pain in big toe, can't walk
history.hpi: Woke at 3 AM with excruciating right great toe pain. Toe red, swollen, extremely tender - 'can't even tolerate bedsheet touching it.' Sudden onset, no trauma. Similar episode 6 months ago, resolved after 1 week with ibuprofen. Recently started hydrochlorothiazide for hypertension. Attended party yesterday, ate steak and drank 4-5 beers. No fever, no other joint involvement.
history.pmh: Hypertension, obesity (BMI 34), chronic kidney disease stage 3
history.medications: Hydrochlorothiazide 25mg daily (started 2 weeks ago), lisinopril 20mg daily, aspirin 81mg daily
history.social: Drinks 3-4 beers daily, diet high in red meat, sedentary

physical_exam.right_foot: First MTP joint markedly erythematous, swollen, warm, exquisitely tender to light touch. Limited ROM due to pain. No puncture wounds.
physical_exam.general: Overweight man in obvious pain, limping

imaging.foot_xray: Soft tissue swelling first MTP, no fracture. No erosions or tophi (early disease).
imaging.arthrocentesis: Synovial fluid: yellow, cloudy. WBC 25,000/µL (80% PMNs). Negative Gram stain. Polarized microscopy: needle-shaped negatively birefringent crystals (monosodium urate).

differential: Septic arthritis (but afebrile, crystals on fluid analysis, negative Gram stain)
Pseudogout (CPPD) - but positively birefringent rhomboid crystals
cases.explanation: Gout is crystal-induced arthropathy from monosodium urate crystal deposition in joints due to hyperuricemia (uric acid >7 mg/dL). Acute attack (podagra): sudden, severe monoarticular arthritis, most commonly 1st MTP (50% of first attacks). Classic: wakes patient from sleep, peak pain 12-24 hours, exquisitely tender, red, swollen. Precipitants: alcohol, red meat, seafood, dehydration, diuretics (thiazides), trauma. Synovial fluid analysis: gold standard - needle-shaped negatively birefringent crystals. Risk factors: male, age >40, obesity, CKD, hypertension, alcohol, high-purine diet.
management_pearls: Acute attack: NSAIDs (indomethacin 50mg TID or ibuprofen 800mg TID) - first-line if no contraindications (this patient has CKD - caution)
Alternative: Colchicine 1.2mg x1, then 0.6mg 1 hour later (lower dose than old regimen, fewer GI side effects)
Prednisone 40mg daily x 5 days if NSAIDs/colchicine contraindicated
This patient (CKD): prednisone preferred over NSAIDs
Joint aspiration: if first attack or concern for septic arthritis - send for cell count, Gram stain, culture, crystal analysis
Do NOT start allopurinol during acute attack (can worsen/prolong attack)
Prophylaxis: colchicine 0.6mg daily during initiation of urate-lowering therapy
Lifestyle: limit alcohol, red meat, seafood; increase water intake; weight loss
pitfalls: Septic arthritis: can coexist with gout (10%) - if fever, toxic appearance, high synovial WBC (>50,000), positive Gram stain → treat as septic
Serum uric acid during attack: may be normal (30% of acute gout) - not diagnostic, crystals are gold standard
Urate-lowering therapy (allopurinol): start AFTER acute attack resolves (2-4 weeks), use prophylactic colchicine x 6 months to prevent flares
Thiazide diuretics: increase uric acid - consider alternative antihypertensive (switch to losartan which is uricosuric)
Polyarticular gout: more severe, multiple joints - may need systemic steroids
Chronic tophaceous gout: subcutaneous tophi, erosions on XR - needs urate-lowering therapy (allopurinol, febuxostat)

cases.title: Persistent Dry Cough and Weight Loss
learning_objectives: Understand TB screening and diagnostic approach
Interpret chest imaging findings of TB
Manage active TB with appropriate isolation and treatment
cases.presentation: 38-year-old with persistent cough, night sweats, and 15-pound weight loss over 3 months

history.chief_complaint: Cough that won't go away, losing weight
history.hpi: Persistent cough for 3 months, initially dry, now productive of yellow sputum, occasionally blood-tinged. Night sweats requiring change of clothes 3-4x/week. Unintentional 15-pound weight loss despite normal appetite. Low-grade fevers. Fatigue. No chest pain, no dyspnea at rest. Treated with 2 courses of antibiotics (azithromycin, amoxicillin) without improvement. Recent immigrant from Philippines (arrived 6 months ago). Lives in crowded shelter.
history.pmh: No known medical problems, never had TB testing
history.social: Recent immigrant, lives in homeless shelter, no smoking/alcohol/drugs
history.family: Brother in Philippines had lung disease (details unknown)

physical_exam.vitals: Temp 100.8°F, HR 92, BP 108/68, RR 18, O2 sat 96% on RA, Weight 138 lbs (was 153 lbs 3 months ago)
physical_exam.lungs: Decreased breath sounds right upper lobe, occasional crackles. No wheezes.

labs.sputum_afb_smear: Positive for acid-fast bacilli (3 sputum samples)
labs.sputum_culture: Pending (takes 6-8 weeks), will show M. tuberculosis

imaging.chest_xray: Right upper lobe cavitary lesion with surrounding infiltrate. Hilar lymphadenopathy. No pleural effusion.
imaging.ct_chest: Confirms cavitary lesion RUL, tree-in-bud opacities suggesting endobronchial spread

differential: Lung cancer (weight loss, hemoptysis, but young age, positive AFB smear)
Lung abscess (cavitary lesion but AFB positive)
Atypical mycobacterial infection (NTM) - similar presentation, slower progression
Fungal infection (histoplasmosis, coccidioidomycosis) - endemic areas, different imaging
Sarcoidosis (hilar LAD, but cavitation rare, no AFB)
cases.explanation: Pulmonary tuberculosis (TB) is infectious disease caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis transmitted via respiratory droplets. Active TB: persistent cough >3 weeks, hemoptysis, night sweats, weight loss, fever. High-risk: immigrants from endemic areas, HIV, homelessness, incarceration, immunosuppression. Classic CXR: upper lobe infiltrates with cavitation (high oxygen tension favors TB growth). Diagnosis: sputum AFB smear (rapid but less sensitive), culture (gold standard, 6-8 weeks), nucleic acid amplification (rapid). Airborne isolation required - highly contagious.
management_pearls: IMMEDIATE airborne isolation (negative pressure room, N95 masks)
Report to public health department (notifiable disease)
Directly Observed Therapy (DOT) - ensure compliance
Standard 4-drug regimen (RIPE): Rifampin, Isoniazid, Pyrazinamide, Ethambutol - daily x 8 weeks (intensive phase)
Continuation phase: Rifampin + Isoniazid x 18 weeks (total 6 months if no complications)
Pyridoxine (vitamin B6) 25-50mg daily with isoniazid (prevent peripheral neuropathy)
Baseline labs: hepatic panel, creatinine, CBC, HIV test
Monitor: monthly LFTs (hepatotoxicity risk), visual acuity (ethambutol optic neuritis)
Contact investigation: test close contacts, household members
pitfalls: Drug resistance: multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB) resistant to rifampin and isoniazid - needs susceptibility testing, modified regimen x 18-24 months
Hepatotoxicity: rifampin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide all hepatotoxic - monitor LFTs monthly, hold drugs if ALT >5x ULN
Ethambutol: optic neuritis (decreased red-green color vision, decreased acuity) - baseline and monthly eye exams
Rifampin drug interactions: potent CYP450 inducer, decreases levels of many drugs (OCPs, warfarin, antiretrovirals)
Paradoxical reaction: worsening symptoms/imaging 2-3 months into treatment due to immune reconstitution - continue treatment, add steroids if severe
Latent TB: positive IGRA/PPD, negative CXR, asymptomatic - treat with 3-4 months rifampin or 9 months isoniazid to prevent active disease

cases.title: Severe Abdominal Pain and Vomiting
learning_objectives: Understand diagnostic criteria and severity assessment
cases.presentation: 46-year-old with severe epigastric pain radiating to back, nausea, and vomiting for 12 hours

history.chief_complaint: Severe stomach pain, can't keep anything down
history.hpi: Sudden onset severe epigastric pain starting last night after large meal. 10/10 severity, constant, boring quality, radiates straight through to back. Multiple episodes vomiting, no relief after vomiting. Unable to eat or drink. Pain worse lying flat, slightly better leaning forward. No fever at home. Previous similar episode 1 year ago (milder, resolved spontaneously). History of gallstones, awaiting cholecystectomy.
history.social: Denies alcohol use, non-smoker

physical_exam.vitals: Temp 100.2°F, HR 108, BP 102/68, RR 22, O2 sat 96% on RA
physical_exam.general: Appears ill, in significant distress, lying still
physical_exam.abdomen: Epigastric tenderness, mild distention. Hypoactive bowel sounds. No rebound or guarding. No masses. No Grey Turner or Cullen signs.

labs.lfts: AST 245 U/L, ALT 312 U/L, Alk Phos 178 U/L, T bili 1.8 mg/dL - suggest gallstone etiology

imaging.ruq_ultrasound: Multiple gallstones, no CBD dilation. Cannot visualize pancreas (bowel gas)
imaging.ct_abdomen: Diffuse pancreatic edema and inflammation, peripancreatic fat stranding. No necrosis. Small amount of peripancreatic fluid.

differential: Perforated peptic ulcer (free air on imaging, peritoneal signs)
Mesenteric ischemia (older, AFib, severe pain out of proportion)
Acute cholecystitis (RUQ pain, Murphy's sign, but lipase markedly elevated)
Bowel obstruction (colicky pain, distention, air-fluid levels)
cases.explanation: Acute pancreatitis is inflammation of pancreas from premature activation of digestive enzymes causing autodigestion. Most common causes: gallstones (40%), alcohol (30%), hypertriglyceridemia (>1000 mg/dL). Diagnosis requires 2 of 3: (1) Characteristic abdominal pain, (2) Lipase or amylase >3x ULN, (3) Imaging findings. Severity: Revised Atlanta criteria - mild (no organ failure, no complications), moderate (transient organ failure <48h or local complications), severe (persistent organ failure >48h). Ranson criteria and APACHE II score predict severity.
management_pearls: Aggressive IV fluid resuscitation: LR 250-500 mL/hr (goal UOP >0.5 mL/kg/hr) - most important intervention
NPO initially, pain control (opioids - morphine, hydromorphone)
Antiemetics: ondansetron 4-8mg IV
Early enteral nutrition (within 24-48h): nasogastric or oral diet as tolerated - reduces complications vs TPN
Monitor: q8h lipase, CBC, BMP (watch for hypocalcemia, hyperglycemia, AKI)
Gallstone pancreatitis: ERCP if concurrent cholangitis or persistent CBD obstruction; cholecystectomy same admission once pancreatitis resolves
ICU if severe: persistent organ failure (shock, respiratory failure, AKI), severe hypocalcemia
No antibiotics unless infected necrosis suspected (fever, positive blood cultures after 7-10 days)
pitfalls: Necrotizing pancreatitis: 10-20%, CT shows non-enhancing pancreatic tissue, high mortality - may need intervention (drainage, debridement)
Infected pancreatic necrosis: fever, leukocytosis >7-10 days - needs CT-guided aspiration/culture, antibiotics (carbapenems, fluoroquinolones), possible surgical debridement
Pancreatic pseudocyst: fluid collection >4 weeks, may cause pain, obstruction - intervention if symptomatic
ERCP timing: urgent (<24h) if concurrent cholangitis; otherwise delay until pancreatitis resolves
Hypertriglyceridemia >1000: can cause pancreatitis - treat with insulin drip + fibrates to lower TGs
Hypocalcemia: saponification (calcium binds free fatty acids) - severe <7 mg/dL may need IV calcium

cases.title: Confusion and Decreased Urination
learning_objectives: Differentiate prerenal, intrinsic, and postrenal AKI
Manage volume status and identify reversible causes
cases.presentation: 78-year-old with confusion, decreased urine output, and weakness for 2 days

history.chief_complaint: Not herself, confused, not urinating much
history.hpi: Per daughter: Patient had diarrhea for 5 days (viral gastroenteritis), decreased oral intake. Last 2 days noticed decreased urination, weakness, confusion (doesn't recognize family). Usually very sharp. Taking all her medications as prescribed. No fever currently. Had been taking extra ibuprofen for arthritis pain during illness. Baseline creatinine 1.2 mg/dL 3 months ago.
history.pmh: Hypertension, chronic kidney disease stage 2, osteoarthritis, heart failure (EF 40%)
history.medications: Lisinopril 20mg daily, furosemide 40mg daily, metoprolol 50mg BID, ibuprofen 600mg TID x 5 days
history.social: Lives with daughter, baseline ADLs independent

physical_exam.vitals: Temp 98.2°F, HR 98, BP 98/62 (baseline 130/80), RR 18, O2 sat 96% on RA
physical_exam.heent: Dry mucous membranes, decreased skin turgor
physical_exam.abdomen: Soft, non-tender
physical_exam.neurologic: Confused, oriented to self only, no focal deficits

labs.bmp: Na 148 mEq/L, K 5.4 mEq/L, Cl 110 mEq/L, HCO3 18 mEq/L, BUN 68 mg/dL, Creatinine 3.8 mg/dL (baseline 1.2)
labs.urinalysis: Specific gravity 1.030, no blood, no protein, no casts, few hyaline casts

imaging.renal_ultrasound: Normal-sized kidneys, no hydronephrosis, no stones

differential: Prerenal AKI (volume depletion, hypoperfusion) - most likely given diarrhea, poor PO intake, low FeNa
Acute tubular necrosis (intrinsic) - from prolonged hypoperfusion, NSAIDs, but urine suggests prerenal
Acute interstitial nephritis (drug-induced from NSAIDs/ACEi) - less likely without eosinophiluria/WBC casts
Postrenal AKI (obstruction) - ruled out by ultrasound (no hydronephrosis)
Cardiorenal syndrome (heart failure worsening) - but no volume overload signs
cases.explanation: Acute kidney injury (AKI) is abrupt decline in kidney function - increase in creatinine ≥0.3 mg/dL within 48h or ≥1.5x baseline. Three categories: (1) Prerenal (60-70%): hypoperfusion from volume depletion, heart failure, cirrhosis - FeNa <1%, BUN:Cr >20:1, responds to fluids; (2) Intrinsic (25-40%): ATN, AIN, glomerulonephritis - FeNa >2%, muddy brown casts; (3) Postrenal (5-10%): obstruction - hydronephrosis on imaging. This patient: prerenal from diarrhea/poor PO intake, exacerbated by NSAIDs (reduce renal perfusion), ACE inhibitor, diuretic. FeNa 0.4% confirms prerenal.
management_pearls: STOP nephrotoxins: hold NSAIDs, ACE inhibitor, diuretics temporarily
IV fluid resuscitation: NS or LR bolus 500-1000 mL, then maintenance based on response
Monitor: daily weights, strict I/Os, BMP daily (watch potassium, creatinine)
Foley catheter: accurately measure urine output
Address underlying cause: treat diarrhea, encourage PO intake once alert
Restart home medications gradually once volume repleted and creatinine improving
No dialysis needed if responds to fluids (prerenal)
Nephrology consult if: no response to fluids, creatinine continues rising, hyperkalemia, acidosis, uremic symptoms
pitfalls: Acute tubular necrosis (ATN): if prerenal AKI untreated, progresses to intrinsic injury - FeNa >2%, muddy brown casts, longer recovery
Contrast-induced nephropathy: avoid IV contrast if AKI present - use non-contrast CT or MRI
Hyperkalemia: K >6.5 with ECG changes (peaked T waves, widened QRS) → calcium gluconate, insulin+glucose, albuterol nebulizer, consider dialysis
Uremic symptoms: altered mental status, pericarditis, asterixis → indication for urgent dialysis
Volume overload: if heart failure present, careful fluid resuscitation - may need diuretics once perfusion restored
Medication adjustment: renally-dosed medications (antibiotics, anticoagulants) need dose adjustment for GFR

cases.title: Rash After Starting New Medication
learning_objectives: Differentiate benign rash from severe drug reactions
cases.presentation: 34-year-old with diffuse red rash and itching, started 3 days after beginning antibiotic for UTI

history.chief_complaint: Itchy red rash all over body
history.hpi: Started trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole 7 days ago for UTI (first time taking this medication). Rash appeared 3 days ago, started on trunk, now spreading to arms and legs. Intensely itchy. No pain. No fever. No blisters or skin peeling. UTI symptoms resolved. Took last dose of antibiotic yesterday (completed 7-day course). No previous drug allergies.
history.pmh: Recurrent UTIs, no other medical problems
history.social: Works as teacher, no recent travel

physical_exam.skin: Diffuse erythematous maculopapular rash on trunk, arms, legs. Confluent in areas. No vesicles, no bullae, no mucosal involvement. No Nikolsky sign. Significant excoriations from scratching.
physical_exam.oropharynx: No oral lesions, no mucosal erythema

labs.none_needed: Clinical diagnosis unless severe (then check CBC, CMP, eosinophils)

differential: Viral exanthem (recent illness, but temporal relationship with medication stronger)
Stevens-Johnson syndrome (but no mucosal involvement, no blisters, no systemic symptoms)
DRESS syndrome (drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms - but no fever, no organ involvement)
Urticaria (but fixed lesions, not transient wheals)
cases.explanation: Maculopapular drug eruption (exanthematous drug eruption) is most common type of drug reaction. Typically starts 7-14 days after drug initiation (or 1-3 days if prior exposure). Symmetric, erythematous macules/papules, often confluent, starting on trunk and spreading peripherally. Pruritic. Common culprits: antibiotics (penicillins, sulfonamides, cephalosporins), allopurinol, anticonvulsants. Benign, self-limited - resolves 1-2 weeks after stopping offending drug. Type IV hypersensitivity reaction (T-cell mediated).
management_pearls: STOP offending medication immediately (TMP-SMX in this case)
Symptomatic treatment: oral antihistamines (diphenhydramine 25-50mg q6h or cetirizine 10mg daily)
Topical corticosteroids: triamcinolone 0.1% cream BID for pruritus/inflammation
Cool compresses, oatmeal baths for symptom relief
Oral steroids: if severe or extensive - prednisone 40-60mg daily x 5-7 days, then taper
Document allergy in medical record - avoid TMP-SMX and sulfa-containing drugs in future
Educate: rash may worsen 1-2 days after stopping drug before improving, full resolution takes 1-2 weeks
No need for skin biopsy unless diagnosis uncertain or concerned for severe reaction
pitfalls: Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS)/Toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN): SEVERE reactions - mucosal involvement (oral, ocular, genital erosions), skin blistering, Nikolsky sign positive, fever, systemic toxicity → STOP drug, hospitalize (burn unit), IV fluids, supportive care. High mortality.
DRESS syndrome: fever, facial edema, lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia, organ involvement (hepatitis, nephritis) - starts 2-8 weeks after drug → hospitalize, high-dose steroids
Serum sickness-like reaction: fever, arthralgias, urticarial rash, lymphadenopathy 7-14 days after drug (cefaclor common) → steroids
Cross-reactivity: sulfa antibiotics (TMP-SMX) have low cross-reactivity with other sulfonamides (furosemide, thiazides, sulfonylureas) - allergy to antibiotic doesn't preclude other sulfa drugs
Continuing drug: if rash mild and drug essential, can sometimes continue with monitoring and symptom management - but safest to stop

cases.title: Numb Feet and Burning Sensation
cases.presentation: 62-year-old with numbness and tingling in both feet, burning sensation at night for 6 months

history.chief_complaint: Feet are numb and burn at night
history.hpi: Gradual onset numbness and tingling in both feet over past year, now affecting lower legs. Symmetric. Burning, shooting pain worse at night, interferes with sleep. Feels like 'walking on cotton.' Noticed decreased sensation - didn't feel cut on foot last month until saw blood. Balance problems, especially in dark. No weakness. Longstanding poorly controlled diabetes.
history.pmh: Type 2 diabetes x 15 years (A1c typically 9-10%), hypertension, hyperlipidemia, obesity
history.medications: Metformin 1000mg BID, glipizide 10mg BID, lisinopril 40mg daily, atorvastatin 40mg daily
history.social: Sedentary, poor diet adherence, no alcohol, no smoking
history.family: Father had diabetes, died from complications

physical_exam.vitals: Temp 98.6°F, HR 78, BP 142/88, RR 14, Weight 245 lbs, BMI 36
physical_exam.neurologic_lower_extremities: Decreased sensation to light touch, pinprick, vibration in stocking distribution bilaterally (to mid-calf). Absent ankle reflexes, diminished knee reflexes. Normal strength. Normal proprioception.
physical_exam.feet: Healed ulcer right plantar surface. Thick toenails. Dry skin. Diminished pedal pulses bilaterally.
physical_exam.monofilament_test: Unable to feel 10g monofilament on plantar surfaces bilaterally

imaging.emg_ncs: Shows length-dependent sensory > motor polyneuropathy consistent with diabetic neuropathy (if diagnosis uncertain)

differential: Vitamin B12 deficiency (but level normal, can coexist with diabetes)
Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (CIDP) - progressive weakness, areflexia, elevated CSF protein
Peripheral arterial disease (claudication, but neuropathy more likely with sensory findings)
Spinal stenosis (neurogenic claudication, but symmetric distal findings favor neuropathy)
cases.explanation: Diabetic peripheral neuropathy (DPN) is most common complication of diabetes, affecting 50% of patients with longstanding disease. Pathophysiology: chronic hyperglycemia causes nerve damage via multiple mechanisms (oxidative stress, advanced glycation end products, microvascular ischemia). Classic presentation: symmetric distal sensory polyneuropathy - 'glove and stocking' distribution, loss of protective sensation, neuropathic pain (burning, shooting). Motor involvement less common. Complications: foot ulcers (decreased sensation), falls (proprioception loss), Charcot foot (joint destruction). Risk factors: duration of diabetes, poor glycemic control, hypertension, hyperlipidemia.
management_pearls: PRIMARY: Optimize glucose control - target A1c <7% (only proven intervention to prevent/slow progression)
Neuropathic pain (first-line): Gabapentin 300mg qHS, titrate to 300-600mg TID (max 3600mg/day) OR Pregabalin 75mg BID, titrate to 150-300mg BID
Alternative pain management: Duloxetine 60mg daily (SNRI, FDA-approved for DPN) OR Amitriptyline 25-75mg qHS
Topical: Lidocaine patches 5% or capsaicin cream 0.075% for localized pain
Foot care education: daily inspection, proper footwear, moisturize (not between toes), podiatry referral
Screen for complications: annual monofilament testing, check pedal pulses, inspect for ulcers
Prevent falls: physical therapy, home safety assessment, adequate lighting
Optimize cardiovascular risk: BP <140/90, statin therapy, aspirin
pitfalls: Diabetic foot ulcer: high risk with loss of protective sensation - needs aggressive wound care, offloading, sometimes antibiotics/surgery to prevent amputation
Charcot foot: painless joint destruction, foot deformity, warmth, swelling - needs offloading, immobilization, orthopedic/podiatry referral
Autonomic neuropathy: can coexist - gastroparesis, orthostatic hypotension, erectile dysfunction, neurogenic bladder
Acute painful neuropathy: paradoxical worsening of pain with rapid glucose control ('insulin neuritis') - pain eventually improves but may take months
Opioids: generally avoided for chronic neuropathic pain (limited efficacy, high addiction risk)
Other causes: if atypical features (rapid onset, asymmetric, predominantly motor) - consider alternative diagnoses (B12, thyroid, CIDP, vasculitis)

cases.title: Man with Red, Watery Eye
learning_objectives: Differentiate from bacterial and allergic conjunctivitis
cases.presentation: 28-year-old man with 2 days of red, watery left eye with discharge

history.chief_complaint: My left eye is really red and watery
history.hpi: Woke up 2 days ago with left eye redness and excessive tearing. Watery discharge, eyes stuck together in morning. Gritty sensation but no pain. Vision unchanged. No photophobia. Coworker had similar symptoms last week. Now right eye starting to become red.
history.social: Office worker, wears glasses for distance

physical_exam.eye_exam: Left eye: diffuse conjunctival injection, watery discharge, mild lid edema, palpable preauricular lymph node. Right eye: early conjunctival injection. Visual acuity 20/20 OU. Pupils equal and reactive. No corneal infiltrate on fluorescein staining. No purulent discharge.

cases.explanation: Viral conjunctivitis ('pink eye') most commonly caused by adenovirus. Key features: (1) Watery discharge (vs purulent in bacterial), (2) Preauricular lymphadenopathy (viral marker), (3) Often bilateral or sequentially bilateral, (4) Contact with infected person, (5) No vision loss or severe pain. Highly contagious via direct contact and fomites. Self-limited but lasts 1-3 weeks.
management_pearls: Supportive care: cool compresses 4-5 times daily, preservative-free artificial tears q2-4h
NO ANTIBIOTICS - viral etiology, antibiotics ineffective and promote resistance
Infection control: contagious for 10-14 days from symptom onset
Avoid work/school until discharge resolves (typically 7-10 days minimum)
Hand hygiene: frequent handwashing, avoid touching eyes
Don't share towels, pillowcases, eye makeup, contact lenses
Discard eye makeup and contact lenses used during infection
Antihistamine drops if concurrent allergy symptoms
pitfalls: Bacterial conjunctivitis: thick purulent (yellow-green) discharge, matting - treat with erythromycin ointment or polymyxin B-trimethoprim drops
Allergic conjunctivitis: bilateral, intense itching, seasonal, chemosis, no lymphadenopathy - treat with antihistamine/mast cell stabilizer drops
Neonatal conjunctivitis (<28 days): concerning for gonorrhea or chlamydia - urgent ophthalmology referral
Red flags requiring ophthalmology referral: severe pain, photophobia, vision loss, corneal opacity, unilateral with vesicular rash (HSV)
Contact lens wearers: remove lenses, consider bacterial/acanthamoeba keratitis if corneal infiltrate

cases.title: Teenager with Worsening Abdominal Pain
learning_objectives: Understand McBurney's point and migration of pain
Apply Alvarado score for risk stratification
cases.presentation: 17-year-old male with 12 hours of progressive right lower quadrant pain

history.chief_complaint: Stomach pain that won't go away
history.hpi: Pain started periumbilically yesterday evening, described as dull ache. Gradually migrated to right lower quadrant overnight and now sharper. Associated with nausea, one episode of vomiting, and anorexia. No diarrhea. Fever developed in last few hours. Unable to find comfortable position. Pain worse with movement and coughing.
history.social: High school student, plays basketball

physical_exam.general: Appears uncomfortable, prefers to lie still
physical_exam.abdomen: Tender at McBurney's point with guarding and rebound tenderness. Positive Rovsing's sign (pain in RLQ with LLQ palpation). Positive psoas sign. Bowel sounds diminished. No masses.

imaging.ct_abdomen_pelvis: Dilated appendix measuring 12mm with periappendiceal fat stranding and fluid. Appendicolith present. Findings consistent with acute appendicitis.

cases.explanation: Acute appendicitis: obstruction of appendiceal lumen → bacterial overgrowth → inflammation → perforation risk. Classic presentation: (1) Pain migration from periumbilical to RLQ (visceral to parietal peritoneum), (2) Anorexia and nausea (almost universal), (3) Fever (usually low-grade), (4) Peritoneal signs (guarding, rebound). Alvarado score >7 suggests high probability. Diagnostic imaging: ultrasound in children/thin adults, CT in adults when diagnosis unclear.
management_pearls: NPO immediately, IV fluids for hydration
Urgent surgical consultation for appendectomy
Antibiotics: Ceftriaxone + metronidazole OR piperacillin-tazobactam (broad spectrum covering GI flora)
Pain management: morphine or hydromorphone (pain control does NOT mask diagnosis)
Laparoscopic appendectomy preferred (less pain, faster recovery) vs open if perforated/abscess
If perforated appendicitis: longer antibiotics (5-7 days), consider interval appendectomy after 6-8 weeks
Time-sensitive: perforation risk increases significantly after 24-36 hours
pitfalls: Atypical presentations: retrocecal appendix (back/flank pain), pelvic appendix (diarrhea, urinary symptoms), pregnancy (displaced by uterus)
Female patients: must rule out ovarian torsion, ectopic pregnancy, PID - pregnancy test mandatory
Perforated appendicitis: sudden improvement in pain (decompression), then diffuse peritonitis
Children <5 and elderly: higher perforation rates due to delayed diagnosis
Conservative management: antibiotics alone successful in 70% but 30% recurrence - reserved for poor surgical candidates

cases.title: Woman with Fatigue and Weight Gain
cases.presentation: 42-year-old woman with 6 months of progressive fatigue, weight gain, and cold intolerance

history.chief_complaint: Always tired and can't lose weight despite trying
history.hpi: Gradual onset of fatigue over 6 months, worse in afternoons. Gained 15 lbs despite no diet changes. Always feels cold, especially hands and feet. Dry skin. Constipation. Hair thinning. Difficulty concentrating at work. Heavy menstrual periods. Denies chest pain, palpitations, or shortness of breath.
history.social: Works as accountant, married with 2 children
history.family: Mother has Hashimoto's thyroiditis, sister has type 1 diabetes

physical_exam.thyroid: Mildly enlarged, firm, non-tender, no nodules
physical_exam.skin: Dry, cool, slight yellowing of palms
physical_exam.extremities: Non-pitting edema, delayed relaxation phase of ankle reflexes

imaging.none: Thyroid ultrasound not needed for diagnosis unless nodules palpated

cases.explanation: Primary hypothyroidism: thyroid gland failure, most commonly autoimmune (Hashimoto's thyroiditis) in US. Elevated TSH + low free T4 confirms primary hypothyroidism. Positive TPO antibodies indicate Hashimoto's. Clinical features result from decreased metabolism: fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance, constipation, bradycardia, delayed reflexes. Hair thinning, dry skin, menorrhagia common. Strong family history (autoimmune diseases cluster).
management_pearls: Levothyroxine: start 1.6 mcg/kg/day (typically 50-100 mcg daily), take on empty stomach 30-60 min before breakfast
Goal TSH: 0.5-2.5 mIU/L for most patients
Check TSH after 6-8 weeks, adjust dose by 12.5-25 mcg increments until TSH normalized
Once stable: monitor TSH annually
Patient education: lifelong treatment, consistent timing/brand of medication
Drug interactions: calcium, iron, PPIs decrease absorption - separate by 4 hours
Pregnancy: increase dose by 30% immediately, monitor TSH monthly (higher requirements)
Associated conditions: screen for other autoimmune diseases (celiac, B12 deficiency, vitiligo)
pitfalls: Subclinical hypothyroidism: elevated TSH, normal free T4 - treat if TSH >10, symptomatic, or pregnant/planning pregnancy
Central hypothyroidism: low/normal TSH with low free T4 - pituitary/hypothalamic disease, needs MRI
Overtreatment: iatrogenic hyperthyroidism - palpitations, anxiety, osteoporosis, AFib risk
Elderly: start lower dose (25-50 mcg) to avoid cardiac stress
Myxedema coma: severe hypothyroidism with altered mental status, hypothermia, hypotension - medical emergency
Don't confuse with depression: both cause fatigue, but thyroid causes physical signs

cases.title: Man with Red, Swollen Leg
learning_objectives: Diagnose cellulitis based on clinical features
Differentiate from DVT and other mimics
cases.presentation: 55-year-old man with 3 days of progressive redness, warmth, and swelling of right lower leg

history.chief_complaint: My right leg is red, hot, and swollen
history.hpi: Noticed small cut on shin from gardening 5 days ago. Three days ago, area became red, warm, painful. Redness spreading up leg. Leg now very swollen. Fevers to 101°F. Unable to bear weight due to pain. No chest pain or shortness of breath.
history.social: Works outdoors, recent gardening. No recent travel.

physical_exam.right_leg: Erythema extending from ankle to mid-calf, poorly demarcated borders. Warm to touch. Tender to palpation. Moderate non-pitting edema. Small healing abrasion on shin. No fluctuance or crepitus. Calf swelling but negative Homan's sign.

imaging.none: Clinical diagnosis. Ultrasound if DVT suspected shows no deep vein thrombosis.

cases.explanation: Cellulitis: acute bacterial infection of dermis and subcutaneous tissue. Most common pathogens: Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A Strep), Staphylococcus aureus. Clinical features: (1) Erythema, warmth, edema, tenderness, (2) Poorly defined borders (vs abscess), (3) Systemic symptoms (fever, leukocytosis), (4) Portal of entry (trauma, tinea pedis, venous insufficiency). Risk factors: diabetes, obesity, lymphedema, venous insufficiency, immunosuppression.
management_pearls: Uncomplicated cellulitis: Cephalexin 500mg PO QID x 5-7 days OR Clindamycin 300-450mg PO TID (if penicillin allergy)
MRSA risk factors (abscess, recent antibiotics, IVDU, endemic area): Add coverage - TMP-SMX DS BID + Cephalexin OR Doxycycline 100mg BID
Severe/hospitalized: IV Cefazolin 1-2g q8h OR Vancomycin 15-20mg/kg q8-12h (if MRSA risk)
Mark borders with pen to track progression/improvement
Elevation of affected limb above heart level
Treat underlying conditions: control diabetes, treat tinea pedis (athlete's foot)
NSAIDs for pain and inflammation
Expected improvement within 24-48 hours - if worsening, consider resistance or alternative diagnosis
pitfalls: DVT mimics cellulitis: unilateral leg swelling, calf tenderness - need ultrasound to rule out (Wells criteria)
Necrotizing fasciitis: severe pain out of proportion, rapid progression, crepitus, bullae, skin necrosis - surgical emergency
Stasis dermatitis: bilateral, chronic, associated with venous insufficiency, hemosiderin deposition
Purpura fulminans: DIC with purpura, necrosis - meningococcemia or sepsis
Recurrent cellulitis: address predisposing factors (lymphedema, tinea pedis, venous insufficiency), consider suppressive antibiotics
Eosinophilic cellulitis (Wells syndrome): recurrent, eosinophilia, responds to steroids

cases.title: Man with Sudden Severe Big Toe Pain
learning_objectives: Understand role of joint aspiration and crystal analysis
cases.presentation: 52-year-old man awakens with excruciating pain in right big toe

history.chief_complaint: Worst pain ever in my big toe, can't even touch it
history.hpi: Went to bed feeling fine. Woke up at 3 AM with sudden, severe pain in right great toe. Pain 10/10, throbbing. Cannot tolerate bed sheets touching toe. Toe red and swollen. Similar episode 6 months ago that resolved on its own. Had steak and several beers at BBQ yesterday. No trauma.
history.social: Drinks 3-4 beers daily, diet high in red meat

physical_exam.right_first_mtp: Exquisitely tender, erythematous, swollen, warm. Cannot tolerate light touch. Limited range of motion due to pain.

labs.uric_acid: 9.5 mg/dL (elevated, but can be normal during acute attack)
labs.joint_aspiration: Synovial fluid: 25,000 WBC, negatively birefringent needle-shaped crystals (monosodium urate) under polarized light microscopy. Gram stain negative.

imaging.xray_foot: Soft tissue swelling, no erosions (early disease). Chronic gout shows 'punched out' erosions with overhanging edges.

cases.explanation: Acute gout: monosodium urate crystal deposition in joint due to hyperuricemia. Classic presentation: podagra (1st MTP joint, 50% of initial attacks), sudden onset (overnight), severe pain, erythema, swelling. Crystal deposition triggers intense inflammatory response. Risk factors: hyperuricemia, male gender, alcohol (especially beer), purine-rich diet (red meat, seafood), diuretics, CKD. Definitive diagnosis: negatively birefringent needle-shaped crystals in joint fluid.
management_pearls: Acute attack treatment (start within 24 hours for best response):
Option 1: NSAIDs - Indomethacin 50mg TID or Naproxen 500mg BID until resolution (7-10 days)
Option 2: Colchicine 1.2mg at onset, then 0.6mg 1 hour later, then 0.6mg daily (lower GI side effects than high-dose regimen)
Option 3: Corticosteroids - Prednisone 40mg daily x 5 days, then taper (if NSAIDs contraindicated)
DO NOT start allopurinol during acute attack (can prolong/worsen attack)
After attack resolves (2-4 weeks): Start urate-lowering therapy if: recurrent attacks (≥2/year), tophi, chronic arthropathy, or urolithiasis
Prophylaxis when starting allopurinol: Colchicine 0.6mg daily x 6 months to prevent flares
Long-term management: Allopurinol start 100mg daily, titrate to goal uric acid <6 mg/dL
Lifestyle: limit alcohol (especially beer), reduce red meat/seafood, stay hydrated, weight loss
pitfalls: Septic arthritis mimics gout: must aspirate joint if any doubt - fever, single joint, ill-appearing. Gram stain/culture mandatory.
Pseudogout (CPPD): calcium pyrophosphate crystals (positively birefringent, rhomboid), typically larger joints (knee, wrist), older patients
Uric acid level misleading: can be normal during acute attack (25-40% of cases) due to urinary excretion during inflammation
Polyarticular gout: affects multiple joints, can mimic RA or septic arthritis
Tumor lysis syndrome: massive hyperuricemia from chemotherapy, can cause gout
Stop diuretics if possible: thiazides and furosemide increase uric acid

cases.title: Young Woman with Burning Urination
cases.presentation: 24-year-old woman with 2 days of dysuria and urinary frequency

history.chief_complaint: Burning when I pee and going every hour
history.hpi: Started 2 days ago with urgency and frequency. Now burning/pain with urination. Feels like bladder never empties. No gross hematuria but urine appears cloudy. Mild suprapubic discomfort. No fever, chills, back pain, or vaginal symptoms. Recently sexually active with new partner.
history.pmh: No significant history, 2 UTIs in past 3 years
history.social: Sexually active, uses OCPs for contraception

physical_exam.abdomen: Mild suprapubic tenderness, no CVA tenderness
physical_exam.pelvic: No vaginal discharge, no cervical motion tenderness

labs.urinalysis: Color: cloudy. pH 6.5. Positive leukocyte esterase, positive nitrites. WBC >50/hpf. RBC 10-25/hpf. Bacteria many. No casts.
labs.urine_culture: Pending - will show >100,000 CFU/mL E. coli

cases.explanation: Uncomplicated cystitis: bladder infection in healthy, non-pregnant women. Most common pathogen: E. coli (80-85%), followed by Staph saprophyticus, Klebsiella. Clinical diagnosis: dysuria, frequency, urgency, suprapubic pain. UA confirms: pyuria (WBCs), bacteriuria, positive nitrites (gram-negative bacteria). Positive leukocyte esterase indicates WBCs. Risk factors: sexual activity, spermicide use, delayed post-coital voiding, anatomic factors.
management_pearls: First-line therapy (3-day course for uncomplicated):
- Nitrofurantoin monohydrate 100mg PO BID x 5 days (preferred: minimal resistance, low collateral damage)
- TMP-SMX DS PO BID x 3 days (if local resistance <20%)
- Fosfomycin 3g PO single dose (convenient but less effective)
Second-line: Fluoroquinolone (ciprofloxacin 250mg BID x 3 days) - reserve for pyelonephritis or complicated UTI
Phenazopyridine (pyridium) 200mg TID x 2 days for dysuria symptom relief (warn: orange urine)
Adequate hydration
Urine culture not needed for uncomplicated UTI unless: no improvement in 48-72h, recurrent infections, unusual symptoms
Prevention: post-coital voiding, adequate hydration, avoid spermicides, cranberry products may help
pitfalls: Pyelonephritis: fever, flank pain, CVA tenderness, nausea/vomiting - needs longer treatment (7-14 days) ± hospitalization
Complicated UTI: men, pregnancy, catheter, anatomic abnormality, immunosuppression, recent antibiotics - needs culture and longer treatment
Asymptomatic bacteriuria: positive culture without symptoms - DO NOT treat (except in pregnancy)
Vaginitis vs UTI: vaginal discharge, odor, pruritus suggest vaginitis - needs pelvic exam and wet mount
STI urethritis: urethral discharge, partner symptoms, risk factors - test for gonorrhea/chlamydia
Recurrent UTI (≥3 in 12 months): consider suppressive antibiotics, post-coital prophylaxis, investigate anatomic causes

cases.title: Woman with Severe Throbbing Headache
cases.presentation: 32-year-old woman with severe unilateral throbbing headache, nausea, and photophobia

history.chief_complaint: Terrible headache on left side with nausea
history.hpi: Headache started 6 hours ago, gradually worsening. Throbbing quality, left temple and eye. Nausea with one episode of vomiting. Light and noise bothersome - in dark room. Saw flashing lights before headache started. Similar headaches 2-3 times per month for years. Usually triggered by stress, lack of sleep, or menstruation. Ibuprofen sometimes helps if caught early.
history.social: High-stress job as attorney, poor sleep

physical_exam.neuro: Alert and oriented. CN II-XII intact. Motor 5/5 throughout. Sensation intact. Reflexes 2+ and symmetric. Negative Romberg. Normal gait when can tolerate standing.

labs.none: Not indicated for typical migraine with normal exam

imaging.none: MRI brain not indicated for typical migraine pattern with normal neurologic exam. Consider imaging if: new-onset, changed pattern, focal neurologic signs, or red flags.

cases.explanation: Migraine: recurrent primary headache disorder. Diagnostic criteria (ICHD-3): ≥5 attacks lasting 4-72 hours with ≥2 of (unilateral, pulsating, moderate-severe intensity, aggravated by activity) AND ≥1 of (nausea/vomiting, photophobia + phonophobia). Migraine with aura: visual, sensory, or speech symptoms before headache. Pathophysiology: neurovascular disorder with cortical spreading depression, trigeminovascular activation, vasodilation. Strong genetic component. Triggers: hormones, stress, sleep changes, foods, weather.
management_pearls: Acute treatment (early intervention crucial):
- Mild-moderate: NSAIDs (ibuprofen 600-800mg, naproxen 500-550mg) + antiemetic (metoclopramide 10mg)
- Moderate-severe: Triptans - Sumatriptan 50-100mg PO (onset 30-60min) OR Rizatriptan 10mg ODT OR Sumatriptan 6mg SC (fastest onset)
- Alternative: DHE nasal spray, gepants (ubrogepant, rimegepant)
- Antiemetics: Metoclopramide 10mg IV/PO or Prochlorperazine 10mg IV/PO
- IV fluids, dark quiet room, ice pack
Preventive therapy (if ≥4 headache days/month or severe disability):
- First-line: Topiramate 50-100mg daily, Propranolol 80-240mg daily, Amitriptyline 25-150mg qHS
- CGRP monoclonal antibodies: Erenumab, fremanezumab, galcanezumab (monthly injections)
- Botox injections for chronic migraine (≥15 headache days/month)
Lifestyle: identify/avoid triggers, regular sleep, hydration, stress management, limit caffeine
pitfalls: Medication overuse headache: using acute medications >10 days/month causes rebound headaches - withdraw offending agent
Contraindications to triptans: coronary artery disease, uncontrolled hypertension, hemiplegic migraine, basilar migraine
Estrogen-containing OCPs: increased stroke risk in migraine with aura - consider progesterone-only contraception
Red flags requiring imaging: sudden onset 'thunderclap', new-onset after age 50, progressive worsening, focal neurologic signs, fever/stiff neck
Status migrainosus: migraine >72 hours - may need IV DHE or steroid burst
Pregnancy: avoid most medications - acetaminophen + metoclopramide safe, consider nerve blocks
